summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the amount of income tax paid by the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the accrued interests were liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Wealth tax Officer. In reference, the High Court held that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued 'interest on the money lending investment could not be included. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The computation of the net wealth of an assessee calls for a determination of his assets and debts as on the valuation date. [310E] 2. The concept of the value of a property, on a legal plane, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of the assessee. That appears plainly from the definition or "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value". of all the assets belonging to the assessee on the valu date. All the assets, of the assesseefor, bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be taken into account and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounts or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accountancy adopted by the assesses. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (1) of section 7 as the estimated price which, in the opinion of the wealth Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the value date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset. When we speak of the valuation of a Property, on the legal plane there is an obvious advantage in adopting as the valuation dates the last day of a period which is also the relevant period under the Income Tax Act. The reasons for defining the valuation point in terms of the last date of the income tax "previous year" stop there. [309F H] Vedreva Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax, ; , followed. Vedrevu Venkappa Reddy (P) Ltd.

The respondent was charge sheeted for mis conduct in the pay ment of Rs.5,000/ on the ground that he had entered the name of Ashok Kumar in the Pay Roll for May 1969 and that he was not working in that Division. The Enquiry Officer held that the respond ent had entered into the name with Ashok Kumar and that it cannot be termed as a 'semi nation ' because he had not been given any work done by Ashok Kumar. He, therefore, imposed a penalty of stoppage of his five increments which he earned for a period of five years in terms of clause (iv) of Rule 11 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The respondent filed an appeal before the Central Administrative Tribunal contending that since he was found guilty of entering the name in the said pay roll for May, 1969 and so far as other evidence against him was concerned, it could not be termed a 'failure to carry out the said finding. The Tribunal held that there was no violation of the rules of natural justice. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the responde nt. In the appeal before this Court, on behalf of the appella nt, it was contended that the respondent had entered in the name and he had been working in a different Division and therefore he should not be given any lesser punishment than what was found to be non exist ence or irrelevant if another person was found involved to decide whether the sentence imposed, when the findings were recorded, would be justified. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal imposing a lesser penalty on the responden ts cannot, therefore. exercise its power of an industrial court for giving appropriate punishment to him. [27F] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent has not been found guilty by the Tribunal. The Tribu nal also cannot interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the competent authority is based on evidence even if some of it is found to he irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. This Court, in Dhirajlal Girdhari Lal vs Commissioner of Income Tax, ; , held that where the person, without enquiry is di rected, removed or reduced in rank solely on the basis of conviction by a criminal court, the Tribunal may examine the adequacy of the penalty imposed in the light of the evidence and sentence inflicted on the person.

The appellant plaintiff instituted a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from interfering with his possession of the suit property. The respondents contended that he was the lessee in respect of seven lots on an annual rent of Rs. 3600 payable in advance in three instalments; that he had paid the rent upto the end of December 1967, and that the first installment of 1968 but the owner, defendant No. 1 executed a deed of lease in favour of the latter effective from January 1, 1968. The plaintiff claimed to have assumed possession of 7 lots on the basis of an annual lease dated January 1.1968 without his tenancy having been lawfully terminated. The defendants contended that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as constructive res judicata. The Trial Court upheld the contention and dismissed the suit. The High Court, in appeal, held that the plaintiff was wrongly dispossessed by defendant No 1 by reason of the decree passed by the Civil Court on March 29, 1968 which had become final under section 7(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) on the expiry of the lease at the end Of December 1967 the lease stood terminated by efflux of time and defendant No, 1 could not be evicted therefrom; (ii) on a true construction of the terms of the agreement dated January 7, 1968 the suit land was demised to him and he was in actual possession of it till his possession came to be disturbed; (iii) on expiry of lease at that end of the year 1967 the lessee had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of land within the period allowed by section 18 of the Act and had therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the land in terms of section 58(2); (iv) on January 1 1968 the plaintiff came to court contending that even though his lease was not terminated as provided by section 9 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 till his death he had not been dispossessed; (v) on February 28, 1974 the first respondent filed a suit against the appellant for possession on the ground that he is a lessee in the premises and since he has not been evicted, the tenancy was terminated by defendant 1. Therefore, the question whether defendant No1 was a tenant or deemed tenant was one of fact. The trial court held that (a) the plaintiff had in fact been dispossessed by an act of trespass; (b) the suit for possession was not maintainable and (c) the first appellant had failed to prove that he has in fact bean evicted from the land within three years of the date of his dispossession. On appeal, the High Court held that since the plaintiff 's lease was subsisting on January 7.

The petitioners are daily rated employees. They were paid regular wages for similar work in the construction industry. The State Government issued a notification under section 4 of the , fixing minimum wages payable to the regular employees as unskilled workers. The petitioners challenged the said notification before this Court contending that the unit where the petition ers were working was a factory registered under the Factories Act and that the establishment was a 'industry ' within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the . Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by the Constitution. The princi plete distinction between the job and the duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned with the establishment is that one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsmen is equal to the other in the performance of his work. [667B C] 1.2 The principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitution which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. [668D E] 1:3 The principle is not only a comparison of physical activity, but also a comparison made with counterparts in other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical vicinity though owned by the same master. Unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the similar employer or even the other means, there must be discrimination amongst them by the very means. [669E F] Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. 1:4 The principle laid down in Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers (Recognised) vs Union Of India, [1987] 2 SCC 288 is that it is open to the State to classify employees on the basis of qualifications, duties and emoluments and gratuity etc. attached to carpenters in regular services. It cannot be evaluated by the mere averments in the self serving affidavits or counter affidavits of the parties. It must be left to be evaluated and determined by expert body. The principal claim of the petitioners therefore fails and is rejected. [670B C, G H] 2.1 In service jurisprudence, as a Directive Principle of State Policy, there is no absolute application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is not just a comparison or physical activity. It requires the consideration of various dimensions of the job. The accuracy required by the job, and the dexterity it entails may differ from job to job.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. for the murder of one Malan, daughter of the deceased, and sentenced him to undergo life imprisonment under section 201 read with Section 34 I P.C., on the allegation that in pursuance of a conspiracy to commit murders of young girls and women in the vicinity of Babultara village by inflicting injuries on the private parts of the victims or disfiguring their faces in order to make it appear that the accused in the Manwath murders case were not the real culprits. The High Court, however, acquitted accused 5 and 6 of charge No. 1 framed against them under section 148 I. P. C. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the conviction of the appellant alone for conspiracy under section 120B I.p.C was unsustainable in law as at least two persons were required to be involved in the conspiracy and in pursuance thereof they committed the murder. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that accused 6 who had been tried along with accused 5 had been acquitted by the High Court of the charge of conspiracy under Section 302 readwith section 120 B I.PC. and accused 5 was not charged for the offence of murder of Malan. [785B C] 2. The appellant accused 5, 6 and 7 were convicted only for conspiracy u/s 302 read along with section 120(B I P C. The evidence of the approver P.W. 1 and the retracted confession of the accused 5 in holding that the guilt of accused 6 for the murders of Malas was proved beyond all reasonable doubt is not sufficient to establish beyond reasonable doubt that accused No. 6 was found in the company of accused 7 and the approver had been falsely implicated in the charge sheet filed against them u/ss 302 read w.e.f. 2 1 1976. [783C D] 3. The conviction of accused No 5 alone for the conspiracy u /s 302 I.Ps. cannot be sustained. The confession of Accused 5 could have been relied upon by the prosecution to convict him under section 34 read with s.120B I .P. C., but it was not made in any way connected with the offence committed and the conviction was based on such retracted judicial confessions of accused Nos. 5. [784E F] 4. The accused 5 has been rightly convicted and sentence awarded to him u/S 302 read alongwith section 120A I.I.P., C.

The appellant executed a will in 1945 bequeathing all his half share of the properties to his wife, his son and daughter. The testator 's son died in 1947 leaving behind him his adopted son, the appellant and two daughters. The widow of the testator filed a suit for possession of the said properties on the ground that the testator had no power of attorney in respect of the same. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the will was genuine and valid and that the appellant had failed to establish that the execution of the will had been duly proved. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Courts were not justified in recording a finding on two issues in the present case, namely, (1) whether the testator 'became into possession of his properties under his control even before the death of the testatrix and (2) whether he had failed in proving that the property was the last will of the deceased. The question as to when and how the execution was effected was a matter of great importance. Parker vs Felgund, , referred to. Held, further, that it is well settled that where there are two attesting witnesses who have seen the execution, they must satisfy the conscience of the court that the instrument propounded is the last Will of the executant and that it would be sufficient if executed by the testator to remove all clouds and satisfy the mind of the Court that the document propounded was the first will of a free and capable testator '. The test as to whether the execution is proved to be the last and correct one is whether the propounder has taken a prominent part in the execution.

The appellant company was manufacturing Arc Carbons, known as "Cinema Arc Pakistan" and was selling it to persons other than those who ran Cinemas or for any other use. The goods were sold by the appellant company to persons who ran cinemas or to any other uses. The sales tax authorities held that they fell under entry No. 4 of the first schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 and therefore the appellant was liable to pay sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fall under Entry No.4 of Schedule 1 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the State 's appeal without taking further evidence. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the entry in question was not "agricultural machinery" within the meaning of entry 9 of Schedule I of the Madras General Sales tax Act, but was a mere copper rods which were melted by electrical power in the process of welding. The State of Andhra Pradesh contended that the goods fell under Entry 41 of Schedule l of the Central Sales Tax and as such liable to sales tax. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [562F] 2. The term "accessory" is use in the Schedule to describe the goods which might have been produced for use. It is its general or predominant user which seems to determine the category in which an article will fall. The first entry in the schedules relates to "motor vehicles" and includes "component parts of motor vehicles". Entry 9 in schedule 1 relates to 'motor vehicle ' and includes 'electrical instruments, projectors, and sound recording and entry No 11 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry NO. 11 for sound transmitting equipment such as telephones and loud speakers. [562G H] 3. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon ares belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed, is evident from the fact that the term " accessories" has been employed in the market. [563A B] 4. The definition of "accessors" is given under section 3A of the . The sense in Which the word accessories are to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use there with" has, been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. For instance, in entry No 5 the expression occurs at the end as follows; "parts thereof". "supplementary or secondary to something of greater or primary importance", "additional"; "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ." "A sense inwhich the word appurtenant is used, is given. " [563B C] 5. The meaning of this entry can only be satisfactorily determined in the light of the language of the entry itself considered in the context in which it occurs. The entry in respect of "m motorinema" occurs in a schedule in which descriptions of goods to be taxation indicate that, the expression 'required ' is given In Webster ' 's third New International dictionary as follows : "all object or devicethat is not necessary in itself, but that added to the entry 9 in the Madras Act.

The Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966 were framed by the State Government in exercise of its powers conferred under section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957. The Rules were amended with effect from 1st July 1985. Rule 21 of the Rules provided that no quarry lease shall be granted for more than one mineral concession granted under the Rules. Rule 22 provides that no royalty shall be charged from Nimbha das of village potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year. Rule 23A provides that the holder of a Parwana granted under these rules shall pay royalty at the rate of 50% of the royalty payable by the lessees and no royalty is payable by village potter or sub lessee from the lessee, owner, contractor or sub lease holder. The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of Rule 21 on the ground that it was discriminatory inasmuch as it was being treated as part of a consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the state. It was contended that since the royalty was being levied at the rates prescribed under the Second Schedule to the Act, the levy was bad; that the provisions of Rule 23B were not applicable to quarry leases and that section 15 was discriminatory in character. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In these appeals it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the royalty levied on the extracted mineral was in the nature of a tax and it was not in the form of fee which could be used only for specific purposes; (ii) the Act had been passed for purposes of regulation and development of minerals, and (iii) the levy of royalty was discriminatory. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The levy is made under a law made by the Central Government to provide for in any way the freedom guaranteed under Article 301 of the Constitution regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying or excavating minor mineral in respect of minerals not exceeding a specified area. Rule 33 A provides that a holder of the Parwana, granted under this rule has to pay royalty on the annual production of these minor minerals. The grant is made subject to the provisions contained in Rule 21. [412B C] 1.2 In the instant case, the payment of royalty in the State of Gujarat on the minor minerals would impose in any manner the freedom under Article 304(b) of the Constitu tion. [414C D] 1:3 The levy was made under the a law making by the appropriate Government for purposes for implementing the policy of the Act under which the Rules are made. It is not an imposition made by a law to make rules equipping minor minerals with building stones, and therefore, the royalty in question would impose. [416D E] 1 :4 In the present case, there was no discrimination between the petitioners and the State. The mineral may be consumed inside the State, and in some cases may latter on be taken outside the State; but the movement outside the state is not the direct consequence of quarrying. [413E F] 2:1.2 The levy of royalties in the present petitions is made by way of a fee which is charged under Rule 21 which says that no mineral stones shall be levied for morethan 5 hectares in case of minor minerals except in the case of ordinary sand, Kankar, Murram and gravel. [411F G] 2.3 The State Government has the power to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the character of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliar Community in Manjakartha of Manjakottai village. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951 and therefore he must be held to be a trustee within section 6 (9). In appeal to this Court, HELD: The phrase "regulated by usage" in section 6 of the Madras Act19 of 1951 means not hereditary. It is now well established that the office of a hereditary trustees is in the nature of property. This is so whether the trustee has a beneficial interest of some sort or not (see Ganesh Chunder Dhur vs Lal Behary, ; , followed. The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". In the present case, the appellant had been elected as trustee by Senganatha Mudaliar community and there was a vacancy and B was elected to that office. It was not possible to say that there was no succession of As office to another when on the expiry of the period for which A was appointed, there is a vacancy. [426 D E] The word 'successor ' in relation thereto in section 2(9), includes even such cases. But the election to the office was for a fixed period of one year and not for life. It could not be said that there is no succession to another.

The prosecution alleged that the deceased was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space and that when he went to the eastern bank of the channel with a knife, he got up and saw the accused running on the eastern side of the road. The younger brother of the deceased who was also sleeping on the western side rushed towards him and tried to escape from behind. He ran to his elder brother who was standing near him. He was already dead. He had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and Pandurangam was asked to lodge information at the police station which he did. The doctor (PW 16) who held the postmortem examination found nine injuries on the person of the accused. He also described them as incised and four as punctured incised, two more as punctured and the remaining one as a vertical incised wound. He further stated that he had received a "candidate" injury from the side of his father on the ground that he was an absconder. The High Court acquitted the second accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) there was no evidence to show that the present accused was responsible for the death of the victim and Thamizharasan alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Gopi, who was a leper than the deceased; (ii) the High Court erred in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of PW 4 "corroborated by the contents of exhibit P1 (FIR). Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction and sentence of death are set aside. [711E] 2. The evidence of PW4 is not consistent with the version given out by the second appellant in his first information report. He admitted in the course of cross examination that he saw two other persons running ahead of him, but this version appears to be contradicted by the medical evidence. Besides, he has deliberately changed his own stand in court when he deposed that he seen two other person running ahead with accused many others were there and "none of them asked him as to how it had happened". The High court was not even right that PW 4 stood wholly corroborated by the content of the FIR. [612C D] 3. In the first information Report which was very close to the place of occurrence, there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not be sought for. ordinarily in an appeal under article 136 of the Constitution this Court would have hestitated to go into the facts to reappreciate the evidence. It is, however, not possible to adopt that course in this case where the testimony of the sole witness has been rejected with reference to the first appellant who was on the same boat with the appellant. The very fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is definitely an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may not have a qualm of conscience in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the appellant 's father. Apart from that there is a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No. 1 in the site plan. There were also no blood stains on the bench where he was said to be sleeping. [1112F H; 1113A B] 4.

The assessee firm was carrying on business in solicitors. The firm carried on the business of solicitors and other legal representatives. After the death of the firm the arrangement between the various partners in regard to the realisations of the old outstandings was that in respect of the work done by the firm, the realises were to be divided amongst the partners and in respect to the work carried on by the assessee, the newisations were to he divided amongst each partner. The assessee firm paid tax on the profits earned during the assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 and the heirs and legal representatives of the deceased firm were assessed to income tax in the hands of the assessee under section 34(1)(b) read with section 24B of the Income tax Act, 1922. The assessments were challenged by the respondents who were the heirs of the original firm on the ground that they had been assessed to tax for the assessment year 1950 51 and notices for subsequent years were invalid as no income of the Hindu undivided family could be taxed under section 24 B(1) of the Act. Held, that the amounts received by the heirs in the previous year in the present case were not liable to tax as the income received in the year subsequent to the previous or the account year cannot be called income received by them. The provisions of section 24A do not extend to tax liability of the estate of a deceased person beyond the previous, or the accounts year in which that person dies. The fiction is only for a definite purpose and they are limited to the purposes for which they are created and should not be extended beyond that legitimate: field. The expression "or any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" in section 24(B) of Income tax, 1922, means that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs and Legal representatives after his death, they are liable to be taxed as income received on the death. The words "if he has not died", in section 25B(1), refer only to cases provided in the three sub sections of section24B and cannot be extended to cases where a person dies before the publication of the notice under section 22(1). Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd. vs The State of Bihar, [1946] 14 I.T.R. 10, approved.

The petitioners were appointed between December 27, 1956 and July 4, 1968. They were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad. On January 19, 1969 leaders of all political parties in the Legislature of the Andhra Pradesh State appeared to have met and reached the decision that to Implement what are called Telengana Safeguards ', the following measures should be taken : (1) The period of service rendered by each of them should be extended by another five years. (2) The persons who were employed in the ministerial services of the State should be given qualified candidates possessing domicile qualifications and in cases where such candidates are not available the posts shall be left unfilled till qualified domicile candidates become available action on the above lines will be taken immediately. (3) The authorities should consider whether they should be exempted from the operation of section 3 of the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957, and if so, exempt them from the provisions of the Act. (4) The authority should also consider whether the conditions mentioned in the explanation are satisfied. If it is not satisfied that any requirement as to residence within the State or Union territory prior to employment or appointment to an office in that State or union territory is satisfied, the authority may direct the concerned authorities to take action against such persons. (5) The Authority should also examine whether they have been continuously residing within the said area for a period of not less than thirty years immediately preceeding the prescribed date and if it finds that they are not suitable candidates the production before the appointing authority concerned, may be taken forthwith.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post Office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1898 and in two of them he was acquitted by the Additional Sessions Judge but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant had secreted the letters which were in his exclusive possession and that therefore he was being very severely punished. The State appealed to this Court with certificate. It was contended for the appellant that the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from him, it could not be said that there was any prejudice caused to him by the fact that the letters were secreted by him. Held, that the mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. The mere fact of possession does not necessarily imply that the articles were delivered to the dictation of the addressee. In the present case the appellant was given an opportunity to get at the articles and then inferring that he must have utilised the opportunity and was therefore guilty of the offence under section 51 of the Post Offices act. Held further, that in order to establish that the two letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant it is necessary for the prosecution to prove that these letters were delivered by the addressee to the addressees. The fact that a number of articles found in the almirah admittedly belong to the father does not mean merely that the contents of the articles are found in his almirah which, at best, may be regarded as being in the joint possession of himself and his father.

The appellant, a Sub Divisional Magistrate, filed a complaint against the respondents alleging that he had been abused and be laboured by the respondents. The Magistrate ordered that the complaint should be treated as a petition under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947. On appeal, the High Court admitted the application and stayed further proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that no contempt of court had been established because a Court is entitled not to act on an application which is not accompanied by an affidavit properly sworn to or a certified copy of the order. HELD : The High Court should not have drawn an adverse inference from the fact that the reasons for not accepting the prayer for stay were not recorded. [119D] In the instant case, the appellant had admittedly admitted in his deposition that he was informed by the Sub Divisional Officer that he would present whatever he had. According to him, the Panchas did not tell him that his affidavit was not proper. The High court was therefore right in holding that the Sarpanch and the Pan chas had been declared hostile to the respondents and that the matter should be viewed strictly. [120E] Hoshiar Singh vs Gurbachan Singh, A.I.R. 1965 S.C. 1315, followed. In the present case, there was no reason for the High court to have kept in mind the principles which we have mentioned above. [121H; 122A] The High Courts should not be chary of finding a judicial officer guilty of contempt of Court for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the existence of the Order of the High. In such matters those who assert that a person had knowledge about the order must prove this fact beyond all reasonable doubt. If there is any doubt, the benefit ought to be given to the person charged with contempt of the court. If a person bona fide comes to the conclusion on the material placed before him that the source of information is not authentic he cannot be held guilty of Contempt of Court. [122B C] Hoshiarpur Singh vs Mukhtar Singh, ; , referred to.

The appellant was tried for the murder of Sheo Sahai by a constable. The trial court convicted him under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced him to death. On appeal, the High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had no motive to kill Sheo Sahai and that the extra judicial confession made to him by the appellant to a Police Officer was not admissible in evidence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the accused to the police officer was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a direct admission of the appellant 's striking Sheo Sahai with a sword and thereby causing his death. HELD : The High Court erred in rejecting the statement of the accused about the appellant having enmity with him. The confession made by the appel lant to the Police Officer did not amount to a "direct admission of his striking Sheo Rai" of the offence by the prosecution. It was not stated by sub Inspector who recorded the confession that he was taking his bath at night in the Canal distributory and had said that he took his bath there. The evidence about the motive and purchase of the sword show that the appellant had a bath in the canal at that hour. The High court erred in holding that the statement made to the Sub Inspector was admissible under section 32 of the Evidence Act. [205 E F] The evidence of the approver was corroborated by Paley Singh, P.W. 2 and other prosecution witnesses. The Sessions Judge had considered the criticism against the appellant about his confessing to him that he did commit the murder. He had also held that there were good reasons for Ujagar Singh 's not leaving his field whose crops he was watching against the neel gais trespassing and grazing the crop. It is no doubt unusual, as urged for by the counsel for the appellant, that a person who commits a murder in pursuance of an enmity arising out of minor disputes would be feeling so justified in his conduct as to openly admit it to the first person he met and to go to the Panchayat and report about it. It may be that having blurted out the truth to Ujagar Singh when taken by surprise, the appellant thought the best thing to be to proceed to the P. W. 2 's house and report the matter there. It would not therefore be a case of mere suspicion between the appellant and the deceased that he committed the murder and his confession to the Magistrate was false.

The Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls) Rules 1963 were framed by the State Government under section 23(3) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1956. The Rules provided that the electoral roll for a local authority shall be prepared on the basis of the electoral rolls in accordance with Rule 4(1). Under Rule 4 (1) of Rules, the electoral Roll for a Municipal Corporation shall be submitted to the State Election Commission and the list of candidates who had not been included in the electoral list was published on November 16, 1978. The final list of the candidates for election with their symbols was published by the Returning officer on November 25, 1978, notifying that the poll would take place on December 31, 1978 in all the constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants were called upon to submit their claims and/or objections within 20 days from the date of publication of the notice. The respondent No. 2, the Deputy Collector, Raipur, published the electoral ' roll on September 30, 1978 under Rule 4 of the Rules on November 26, 1978 notifying that a poll would be held on December 30,1978 in all three constituencies: six petitioners including respondent No S and four petitioners were declared elected. Their names were however not published under Rule 46 of the rules in view of the interim order made by the Court. Thereafter, the Election Commission notified the names of the appellants as also respondents Nos. 1 and 5 respectively. The appellants challenged the validity of the election on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 2(1) and that the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed. The High Court dismissed the petition holding (i) that respondent No 2, who was the Deputy Collec tor had asked petitioner No. S to appear before him on October 30, 17, 1978 and that as he did not produce any evidence in support of his claim, his application was dismissed; (ii) that none of the persons mentioned in Annexure P 7 preferred any claim before respondent No 3 on October 20, 1978; (iii) that no other claims or objections were preferred either on October 21, 1978 or on any other sub sequent date. The writ petition filed by the appellants was therefore dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that since the period of 20 days had been mentioned in the notices issued under rule 4( 1) and also called upon interested persons to prefer claims and objections within a period of 30 days from date of the publication of that notice when sub rule (3) was published, the entire electoral process held on the strength of the defective electoral roll ' could not be challenged. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The power of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of Writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. This rule applies also to a case in which the validity or election to a local Authority is challenged. The question whether in a given case the delay involved is such that it dissentients a person to relief under Article 22 is a matter within the discretion of the Court which as in all matters of discretion has to exercise it judiciously and reasonably having regard to the surrounding circumstances. [497G H; 497A B] In the instant case, the writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High Courts as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in preferring it.

The appellant was the director of a company which was prosecuted under section 32(5) of the , for failure to comply with the provisions of section 220(1) of that Act. The High Court held that if no general body meeting had been held and the balance sheet and profit and loss account were laid before a general body, there could be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 134(4). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the holding of the annual general meeting and the laying of the balance sheets and profit & loss account before an annual general meetings were a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the Registrar, and (2) the provisions in section 134 were not complied with. HELD : The High Courts had rightly held that the appellant was guilty of offences under sections 32(4) and 134(1)(c). [416 G] (a) Section 134(3) does not contemplate sending of a copy of the account books of the company to the Registrar even without the necessity of their being laid before the general body. The requirement of section 135 is that the balance Sheet and profit or loss account should be sent to the registrar even without necessity of its being laid at the general meeting. Without so laying copies could not be sent for the purpose of section 133(4); (b) Section 135(1), in terms, does not require a copy to be filed with the Registrar and even if they are sent it would not be a compliance with the provision of section 136; (c) Section 32 relates to the preparation of a list of members of the Company and of persons who have ceased to be members as well as a summary, and also provides that it shall be completed within 21 days after the day of first or only ordinary general meeting in the year. [416 A B] (d) The word "shall" in section 135(2), is not mandatory but directory. It is obligatory on the Registrar to send three copies of the accounts and summary, if he does so, to the registered office at the time of the general meetings. If no general meeting is held, the persons concerned cannot be said to have committed a default in complying with those provisions. [417 B C] (e) The provision in section 136(2) that after balance sheet or profit and Loss account or the income and expenditure account, as the case may be, have been laid before, the general election could not, therefore, be held to be illegal. [414 D E] (f) Section 133 of the 1913 Act is a composite one which lays down various requirements which are to be complied with by the company under its first four sub clauses and sub cl. (5) is the penal sub section which penalises the failure to do so. The penalty under this section is for default in filing copies of accounts or the Income and expenditure accounts, as a result of which the balance has not been laid at before the company at the General meeting.

The respondent, a member of the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum, was charged with offences under sections 161 and 165A I.P.C., section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, and section 5 (1) Of the WestBengal Special Courts Ordinance 1949, which provided for the speedier trial of certain offences by Special Courts in respect of which an accused person was being tried under the Special Court. The respondent contended that the Special Courts had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5 of the Act did not empower the State Government to direct a special court to try such offences or classes of cases or classes or cases or class of cases as the State Govern ment could by general or special order make or give effect to the provisions of the Special Act. Held, that the classification implied in this part of section 5 was valid and the Special courts had no power to try all offences or other offences or cases which were committed before the commencement of the Ordinance. The classification implied that the offences and offences which in the opinion of the State government would require speediers trial could be assigned by it to the Special court. The fact that the offence and offences under section 5 were committed in course of the same transaction did not make any difference as regards the nature of the offence or the cases, for, in the absence of any special circumstances which may render the classification invalid, the classification was reasonable and must be upheld. Held further, that section 5 Of the Act was valid. The Special Courts could not therefore try all cases of the offences under the Act and therefore the Special judge had no Jurisdiction to try them.

The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He had joined the post of Associate Professor of Radiology (ex officio) in the Medical College at Rohtak on August 19, 1964. In the absence of any advertisement for the post he was not only holding the post but also performing the teaching experience of the specialist or capacity in which he was working as an Associate Professor. The appellant was selected by the Haryana Public Service Commission for the said post and appointed to the post. He challenged the appointment on the ground that the Selection Committee had no jurisdiction to appoint him to the said posts as he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality as required under the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the post was a clinical post while that of Associate professor of Radiologist was a teaching post and had also the requisite teaching experience while holding the said office. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant is not holding the posts of an Associate professor in the Institute of Radiological College. He, while holding a non teaching post in a teaching hospital like the Irwin Hospital, has been actually teaching the students of the Maulana Nehru Medical College to which it is affiliated. [8E F] 1.2 It is not for the Court to give the appellant promotion or make his appointment to the Post of Associate Professors of Radiotherapy. The Ministry of Health cannot be heard to say that the appellant has not acquired the status of an Assistant Professor of radiology with effect from October 9, 1964 particularly when the Central Government had been utilization of his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of Maulana Gandhi Medical College. [9F G] 1:3.

The workmen of the appellant company were paid minimum wages at the time of the reference. The Company made an industrial dispute before the Tribunal under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for adjudication by the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was no identical industry in this region comparable with the Company and therefore it would be appropriate to fix the minimum wage in respect of the workmen in the company at Rs. 95. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had committed an error of law in not considering the matter as a question of fact. It committed no error in arriving at its decision on that point. [674 E] (ii) The award had to cover the year 1963 64 also and at least for that year the accounts could not possibly have been completed, as that year was still running when the award was given by the tribunal on the 11th January, 1964. Therefore, in fixing the minimum wages of the workman in the Company at Rs 95, it should be deemed to have the same break up. [655 F] (iii) The workmen were not providing any such amenities which were different from those provided by the appellant. In fact, from the Award it appeared that there had been a very considerable rise in the Price Index and the labour had not so far raised a fresh dispute for a further revision of wages over and above the wages fixed by the Industrial Tribunal. [676 G H] (iv) The claim for six months ' wages was not based on any material to show that the Company was providing any amenities which are different from the amenities that were being provided by those concerns in the region which are being charged with the cost of living index and only envisaged that such linking may be permissible by holding that the workmen would automatically get a grant of profit bonus at the rate of six months wages. [677 G H; 677 A] (v) The finding of fact recorded by the Labour Court that there were no other concerns in this country in the same region was not challenged before the High Court. [678 C D] (vi) The Industrial Tribunal had rightly held that the total minimum wage packet of a workman in this company should have been fixed at Rs, 95.

The appellant, a partnership firm, had been assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income tax Officer, Ward A, Muzaffarpur issued to the assessee a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, on June 3, 1966, calling upon it to produce before him its books of account and other relevant papers. The appellant challenged the validity of that notice as well as proceedings taken on the strength of that notices on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The report submitted by the Income tax officer to the Commissioner and the order of the Commissioner were not produced. Therefore, the report submitted under section 151 (2) does not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it is a fit case for issue of notice under s 148. [447 C] (ii) The assessment proceedings are not vitiated by any material before him which could satisfy the requirements Of section 151. [449 E] (iii) The Commissioner has mechanically accorded permission and he did not himself record that he was satisfied that this was a fit one for the issue of a notice. [451 G] (iv) If only he had read the report carefully, he could never have come to the con sider whether this was sufficient for issuing a notice tinder section 148. Further his report mentions "Hence proper investigation regarding these loans is necessary". The report mentions : "Hare cases for investigating as to the truth of the alleged transactions. That is not the same thing as saying that there are reasons to issue, notice under sections 148. 151 and 152(2). [451 H] (v) If the only conclusion is reached on the material before the Income Tax Officer that this is a proper case for the issuing of a show cause notice under S. 148, it just noted the word "yes" and affixed his signatures thereunder.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in soap and umbrella was started in 1945 by an instrument executed on February 7, 1948. The firm carried on the business of manufacturing and umbrella. It had been running its mills at Madras and Bombay and its businesses were split up into two and carried on by two independent partnerships. In 1947 the firm carried out the business in Calcutta and Bombay. For the assessment year 1948 49, the Income tax Officer included the income from business in respect of the profits earned by it during the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and also the Tribunal held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. On reference, the High Court held that there was no succession to the business carried on at the commencement of the Act of 1918 and that the business could be said to have been carried on in Calcutta only when it was discontinued by another person. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The business of the assessee was not a dissolution of the firm but was a business which was taxed under the Indian income tax Act of 1922. [107 D] Under section 25 (4) a mere change in the constitution of the partnership does not count and sections 25(3) and 26(2) do not apply at the same time because, the intention is obviously to keep them separate and when sub section (4), as amended by the addition of the words "unless there has been a succession by virtue of which the provisions of sub section 3 or 4 have been rendered applicable" the assessee cannot be denied the benefit of section 25. [108 E F] The business in question was not discontinued on account of the change in constitution of a partnership, but it was merely a change in its constitution. It was not necessary to consider whether there had been a discontinuance of the business before 1948 or whether there was a succession to that business. [109 G H] In the present case, the business was not even in contemplation of 1922 and the same was not carried on with the object of carrying on the trade within the meaning of section 26(1) of Act of 1947.

The appellant, who was the owner of a house in Bombay, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband and his two sons, and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff 's father had effected a partition of the suit properties between himself and his brothers. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the suit property belonged to joint family; (2) the partition was effected in accordance with the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, and (3) the High Courts had erred in holding that a partition had actually taken place between the plaintiff and his sons. HELD: (i) The finding of the High court that the suit lands belonged to a joint family is essentially a claim to obtain a share in the interest which her husband had in a Mitakshare coparcenary property at the time of his death. [766 B] (ii) The Explanation to section 6 does not apply because the proviso to section six states that the proviso shall not apply where there are two or more coparceners in the joint Hindu family before the death of the person in whose property the heirs claim a share. The Explanation provides that the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in such property that would have been allotted to him if a partition has taken place immediately before his death, and if the statute says that he must imagine a state of affairs in which a little prior to Khandappa 's death, a partition shall be presumed, it cannot be interpreted to mean that having done so, he must cause or permit the imagination to boggle under the oppression of the reality that there is in fact no partition between the appellant and his father. [764 G H] (iii) The explanation to section 3 of the Act does not provide further that the Explanation shall apply only where a partition took place between a deceased person and his heirs immediately before the date of his ' death. The proviso to s 6 does provide that the decision of the appellate authority must turn on the meaning to be given to the said section. [774 A B] In the instant case, the appellant 's suit was based on the provisions Of section 6 which provides that if a person dies during the life time of an intestate his interest in a Mitakshara coparcenary property is at the date when he died, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. The rule of construction embodied in sections 8 and 10 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, is given by this Court in Commissioner of Income tax vs section Teja Singh, ; , followed. (iv) The proviso thereto will further the legislative intent in regard to the enlargement of the share of female heirs, qualitatively and quantitatively. [754 B C] (v) The appellant ' s claim that his father had obtained a share of the interest in the coparcenary property on the hypothesis of a partition between himself & his sons is not correct.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were framed by the Life Insurance Corpora tion of India under section 11(2) of the Life Insur ities Act, 1956. The regulations made thereunder provided that an employee belonging to Class I or Class II appointed to the service of the Corporation on or after 1st September 1956 shall retire on completion of 58 years of age but the appointing authority may, if it is of the opinion that it is in the interest of the corporation to do so, direct such employee to retire on completing 58 years. The respondent was a member of the staff of the appellant Corporation. He was compulsorily retired by the General Insurance Corporation under section II(2). The appellant challenged the validity of Regulation 19(2), inter alia, on the ground that it violated Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the regulations made by the Corporation were not in terms applicable to the transferred employees who became the employees of the respondent Corporation under sub section (1) of section 11 of the Act but only referred to the employees and agents of the Corpora tions who were employed after 1.9. 1956, and that the Regulations made thereunder were not violative of Article 14. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant Corporation that since the regulations had been made in exercise of the power conferred by section 11 (2) the retirement age of employees of its employees was a valid classification and Articles 14 and16 of the Constitu tion had not been violated. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Regulations and other provisions as in force immediately before the commencement of the life insurance Corporation (Amendment) Act, 1981 are binding on the Corporation. [204E] 2.1 Regulation 19 (2), however, has been given retrospective effect from 20th June 1979.

The appellants were charged with contempt of court. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by five members of the Bar Association, Bhiwani to Chandigarh in a closed cover addressed to the Chief Justice for being handed over to him for his personal attention. The appellants took a copy of their letter to the respondent 's counsel and filed an affidavit stating that the High Court had no intention to scandalise the court. In reply the appellants stated that the contents of the letter were correct. The respondent also stated that there was no intention on his part to scandalize the court, nor did he maltreat any public servant or political party or any political party. The contempt proceedings were dropped. The respondents filed an appeal in this Court against the order of the High court. Allowing the appeals, HELD: (1) The High court should have dropped the proceeding and not pursued the matter. [246B] (2) If on facts it appears that the Judge did say things or matters about politics such utterances or views or observations will be the personal opinions expressed by the Judge, and therefore, the protec tive umbrella of the Court cannot be used by way of bringing the critics on the charge of contempt of Court. [245C] (3) If the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer, the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the Court. The reason is obvious. It is no part of the duty of a Judge nor is it a duty in discharge of office of a judge to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. [243E F] (4) If, on facts, it appears from facts that the judge did say anything or matters regarding politics such uttered views or remarks will be his personal opinions or observations would be the Personal opinion expressed by him and, therefore, he is of the view that the matter did not constitute any contempt. [244E F; 244A] (5) If a Judge does say things, or matters, about politics, such utterance or views, will be personal opinions express by the judge, and, in the absence of any finding by the High Courts that the appellants committed any contempt of the court there was never any occasion for acceptance of apology.

The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business in the manufacture of textiles. The company had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had evaded payment of tax. The Income tax Officer assessed the company to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49 but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the company had been assessed to tax under section 5(1) of the Act, and the order was confirmed by the Central Government. On appeal by the appellant the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order on the ground that the provisions of sections 5(2), 6(4), 6 (5) and 7 of the Indian Income tax Act were not applicable to the case. The High Court held that section 5 (1) Of the Act was invalid as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the appellant had been given discriminatory treatment even from those whose cases were referred to under section 3(4) Of Act XXX of 1947 and the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in so far as affected them was not based on a valid classification but only on a rational classification which was rational in view of the objects of the statute. The provisions of section 5 of the impugned act relating to the computation of income were reasonable and did not contravene article 14 Of the Constitution and were void. The procedure prescribed under the Act for reference of the cases to the Commission was substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure provided by the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, which had been adopted in this case.

The appellant Association was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913. The primary objects of the Federation as given in the Memorandum of Association are "to promote Indian business in matters of inland and foreign trade, transport, industry and manufacture, quarries and mines not governed by the . The Federation had a number of establishments known as "Industrial Establishment" which were engaged in the premises in question. The Federation was carrying on a profession as it is "tendering advice to all businessmen and traders". The Federation started its establishment in 1970. The appellant Association filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated February 4, 1964 passed by the Chief Inspector of Shops and Establishments, Delhi, under section 1(4) of the Act, in which the main object of the Organisation was to fall within the definition "commercial establishment" as defined in section 2(5) of that Act. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the activity of the appellant amounted to "work in connection with or incidental or ancillary thereto" and to "any work in connection therewith". In appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the activities of the respondent were not a commercial establishment within the meaning of section 2 (5) as they were not "business" within the expression "commercial Establishment", and (ii) the activity amounted to a 'trade '. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of "commercial establishments" in section2(5), indicates that the activities are connected with trade and business generally. It is an element common to the definitions of " commercial establishment". The expression "business", has been defined in s 2 (g) of Act. In order to fall under the definition of 'commercial establishment ', it must be premises. [354B C] 2. The word "establishment" in s.2(6) of Bombay Shops and Establishment Act, 1954, is not restricted to a business or trade carried on by an individual but includes a shop or a factory registered under that Act and charitable or other trust, whether registered or not which carries on any business, trade or profession or work in connec tion with or ancillary thereof. [355D E] 3. The expression 'business ' has been used in the respective statutes. That was why the question was only of drawing a correct inference about the point in issue from the material already on record. [356F G] 4. The very definition of commercial establishment includes, amongst others, "a business or business". The definition is wide enough to include all kinds of business and income of the association. In the present case, the appellant Association had charitable aims and objects. For all the aforesaid reasons particularly in view of the decision of this Court in R. K. Mittal 's case, it would be necessary to set out the circumstances under which the High Courts were justified in coming to the conclusion that the commercial or industrial inherently falls within the purview of section 1 (4)of the Act. [357H; 354A B] 5. The question is only of getting an establishment or trade or business carried on, or carrying on any other activity carried on. There can be no doubt that the registered office of the Association is premises. charitable or otherwise. It would not take it out of the definition if the activity carried by it amounts to a busi ness. [ 354E F] 6. The mere fact that in the earlier part of the term, the word 'business" has been mentioned as an element of the expression of " Commercial Establishment" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. But putting aside the question whether they carry on a trade or trade would bring it within the ambit of the said clause if the activities carried on are outside the first instance.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family. By a deed dated 7th July 1837, the province of Benaras was ceded to the British Government and the British government granted a sanad of Raj to Raja Chet Singh in perpetuity for a period of 5 years. The income tax authorities held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The High Court on reference held that from the language of the letter dated 7/1837, it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. The appellant contended that the allowance was taxable income under the Indian Income tax Act and not under the definition of agricultural Income tax in section 2(1) of the Act. Held, that the grant of sanad by the appellant was an annual payment of Rs. 2,40,000 to the assessee for life and did no business or obligation. The grant was revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. The allowance was revenue receipt and not taxable income. Commissioner of Income tax, Bihar and Orissa vs Kunwar Sri Trivikram Narain Singh, (1923) L.R. 46 I.A. 225, referred to. Per Sarkar, J. The payment in the instant case was a payment in instalments of the value of the disputed title of the assesses 's predecessor in interest. The payments were made as a percentage of the land revenue collection after deducting cost of Tahsil establishments. The amount which had been received by the successors of the predecessor ininterest of the appellant as compensation for relinquishing his title to the lands was revenue receipts and not income.

The appellants in C.A. No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors Grade 'A ' on various dates in the grade of Supervisor 'A" and were promoted to the post of Chargeman II on compa ny basis. The respondents in CAs Nos. 441/81 and 441/1981 were promoted as Chargeman I in the same grade. On a representation made by them, the Central Administrative Tribunal directed the re spondents to promote them to the next higher posts of Charge Man II with effect from the date they were entitled to seniority. The appellants filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the said order contending that the direction given by the Tribunal was not complied with and that the respondents should be deemed to have been promoted only on completion of 2 years ' service as Supervisor ' A '. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellants that (i) since the order dated 28th December, 1965 which provided a minimum period of service of three years in the lower grade should be fixed for promotion to the higher post, the same having been superseded by the later circular dated 20th January, 1966, the non promotion of the appellants was discriminatory being in violation of Article 16; (ii) since they had not been given the difference of back wages and promotion to higher posts on the basis of their back date promotion as Chargemen II they should be treated as Charge man 'B '. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The order dated 2nd February, 1981 passed by the Central Adminis tration is set aside and the appellants are directed to give the appellants in the said C.As. No 441 of1981 benefit of the directions given by this Court on 2nd Febru ary, 1981. [106G] 1.2 In so far as Supervisors 'A was concerned it has been held that they have been given extra ordinary promotion to be in the teeth of Rule 12 of the Rules and could not confer any legal right on them to be similarly placed. The said decision cannot therefore constitute the basis for an argument that those Supervisors 'B" who had been promoted before the coming into force of the order dat ed 28th Decem ber, 1965 should also be given the same relief which was granted to the appellants earlier in C .A. Nos. 41/81, 1180/81. [107H; 108A B] 1:3 The appellants in CA No. 442/1981 deserve to be granted the same reliefs which were granted by this court to such of the petitioners before that Court wi thout prejudice. [108E F] 2.1 In so doing it would be appropriate that the appellants should give the benefit of their promotion merely on the ground of their seniority as found place in the selection list who could not be promoted to be likewise promoted. The fact that some Supervisors 'C ' had been given higher grade grades and were granted promotion as chargeman II by its judgment dated 4th April, 1983 would not make any difference.

The Central Government specified 50% of the total number of all India Tourist Vehicle permits which may be granted by the Karnataka State Transport Authority. The remaining 50% were to be renewed from one year to three years. The appellants, who were plying tourist vehicles on a route in the State of Karnataka, challenged the grant of permits to the Karnataka state Transport Authority and the Karnataka High Court by its orders dated February 1, 1984 set aside the grant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the preference contemplated by the proviso to section 63(7) of the Act was not available to the State Transport Undertaking; (ii) the State Road Transport Corporation had to be able to operate in the inter state route without detriment to its responsibility for providing efficient and adequate road transport services in any notified area or notified route, and (iii) the grant Of permits having regard to the fact that the permit was granted under section 68F(1), the preference could not be given to operators of tourist cars. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in distinguishing the decision in Sher Singh 's case on the ground that any other interpretation would have wiped out the difference between Chapter IV and Chapter IV A. [1012 B] 2.1 The proviso to Section 63(1) for example provides that other things being equal, a registered cooperative society and a person possessing a licence for driving transport vehicles shall be given preference over individual owners in granting stage carriage permits. The proviso is not expressly referred to in the proviso but it is implicit in the provision that other thing are equal. [1094 C D] 2:2. The expression "tourist cars" as defined in section 2(29 A) of Act, means "a motor car, a motor car or contract carriage, and includes a motor cab, contract carriage and stage carriage". [1014 F G] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. In the instant case, the State transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court have failed to consider the merits of the claims of the Karnataka, State Road Trans port Corporation and the private operators who did not get a certificate of approval from the Central Government because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to s 63(6) of .

The respondent purchased a business carried on by the appellant. The business was transferred to the respondent by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the business. The respondent 's contention was that the transaction was not a sale but only an agreement to pay sales tax and therefore the sales tax due from him could be recovered from him. The Commercial Tax Officer attempted to realise the arrears, but the respondent 'rejected. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Revenue. The single Judge dismissed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. On appeal by special leave, Held: The word 'assessment ' in the scheme of sales tax is a term of varying import. The word is used sometimes to mean the computation of income, sometimes the determination of the amount of tax payable, and sometimes the whole procedure laid down in the Income Tax Act for imposing liability on the tax payer. As the Judicial Committee in Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, , approved. Badrida Pillai vs C .I. T., Bihar ; , referred to. Badrinas Daga v C.l.T. Bihar, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 929 and Badridah vs C,.I.I., Bihar; , , distinguished.

The appellant was appointed senior jailor, Surendranagar District Jail. He was suspended and at the time of the suit he was served with a charge sheet. In substance the charges were that while he was serving as Accountant in the jail, he had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners, maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The trial court found him guilty and convicted him under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the appellant was not concerned with the second contention but it was a dispute between the State of Maharashtra and the respondent State which was reorganised into the two States and the Bombay Refugees Control Reserve to which the State Government had agreed. The Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra vs Abdul Majid, ; , referred to. In the present case, the charge sheet did not mention the fact that the enquiry officer reported that the report of the enquiry held against the appellant had been accepted by the Government and in depriving the respondent of a copy of the report he was handicapped. The State of Bombay vs Abdul Rashid, ; and The State vs Province of East Bengal, ; referred to, distinguished. In view of the fact, that there was no duty cast on the Enquiry Officer to give the appellant with a copy Of the report, he was not entitled to claim a copy thereof. The High Court was right in holding that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant for payment of arrears of salary was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than breach of contract.

The appellants and the respondent were lessees of coal mining rights in the area. The lease was for a period of 20 years and the lessee had surrendered his right to the mine. The appellants filed a suit against the respondents claiming that the intermediate boundary line between the two leaseholds was that of the appellant and the respondents, and that the area encroached upon by them was part of the land leased to the appellants and taken on lease for mining it. The trial court held that the respondent had encroached upon the land and dismissed the suit. On appeal the High Court reversed this finding holding that the appellants had failed to prove that they had knowledge of the sinking of the quarries and pit in the encroached area. Held, that the High court was right in holding that on the facts of the case it could not be said that the respondents had knowledge or knowledge of it since the lease was executed by the appellant. The High Court was wrong in holding otherwise. It is well settled that a map of the document prepared by the parties does not show that the correct boundary line was found in the plot. In the present case the map was drawn to scale and incorporated in the lease deed. The map did not indicate that the survey number was correctly mentioned. The appellant had knowledge about the encroachment only in 1941, but there was no acceptable evidence on their part to establish that they came to know of the removal of coal from the encroached land and that it was purely a question of statutory obligation on the part of them to explain the facts. Talyarkhan vs Gangadas, A.I.R. (1924) Pat. 75, Rangnekar vs Gangdas, A, I. R. (1841) Pat, 760 and Talyakhan vs Gita Das, A., I.R (1923) Pat., 760, referred to.

The appellant, a crosscutter, was in the employ of the respondent company. He was suspended by an order passed under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the same day he terminated his services. The question for determination was whether the action taken under r 18 (a) was bona fide or not. Held, that the appellant could not be said to have taken disciplinary action against him under r, 18 (b). The fact that the proposed enquiry was held would lead to further friction and deterioration in the rank and file of the employees in general and also that maintenance of discipline in the undertaking would be prejudiced if he was retained in service. The appellant could have easily done so by producing two witnesses but withholding the important witnesses on this question, did not amount to denial of reasonable opportunity as the proposed inquiry was bona fides. The fact of the appellant having acted under r., 18 (c) was entirely different from those which applied to an adjudication under section 10 of the Act. The Tribunal had rightly held that the exercise of power was colourable and it could have reasonably been exercised in a case where the termination of service was capricious, arbitrary or unnecessarily harsh on the part of the employer judged by normal standards of a reasonable man that may be cogent evidence of victimisation or unfair labour practice. The Chartered Bank, Bombay vs The Chartered bank Employees ' Union, ; , referred to. Held further, that it is not correct to say that the Industrial Tribunal had taken into consideration the important witness, namely, the Engineer, the Secretary and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value.
