The appellant filed a suit against the receivers of the owners and on August 19, 1954, the receiver granted a lease of the theatre to the appellant. The appellant 's servants and agents were not to have any right to exhibit films in the theatre. The Receiver was not given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses for the film. The trial court passed an order disallowing the objection to the grant of the lease. On appeal, the High Court held that the question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence or to put questions in cross examination of the plaintiff 's witnesses cannot form the subject matter of an issue. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the document could not be permitted to be put to the witnesses who were being examined for film; and that in any event, the trial court had no jurisdiction to record any finding on the issue. HELD : (i) The High Court was invested with power to call for the record of any case decided by any court subordinate to such High Court and in which no appeal lies thereo, if such subordinate court appears (a) to have exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law or to have failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested, or (b) to has acted in the exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity. [439 C D] (ii) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court observed that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import and includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the entire proceedings in a civil court. [441 G] Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, ; , referred to. (iii) The mere recording of a contract between the parties could not affect the jurisdiction of the Court. It was for the trial Court in the first instance to decide that question and there after the High court could, if the matter were brought before it by way of appeal or in exercise of the revisional jurisdiction, have decided that question.

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was working as a Pilot Officer. In 1972 he was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was confirmed on 1st June, 1983. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his termination order contending that he was entitled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th August, 1985. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the respondent was enti tled to be re instated in service notwithstanding the fact that his term of office had come to an end on 30th of August,1985 as stated above and no further order of exten sion had been passed by the Governor. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that he should be deemed to be a regular employee who had a vested right to continue in service beyond 30 years of age. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in disposing of the Writ petition on 24th March, 1988 declaring that the respond ent was entitled for salary upto the period he was enti re to remain in service and further observed that it was open for the opposite parties to consider the claim of the respondent for continuance in service or of fresh appointment and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. [243D] 1.2 The High Courts while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24th3.1988 directed that the re spondent was entitled only to be paid to remain In service and not beyond 30.8.1985 unless there was a further extension. But on 29th March 1985 the services of the first respondent were terminated by the issue of a notice and payment of one month 's salary. The order was to be effective from the date of receipt of termination order and no charges were men tioned therein against the first respond ent. [242E F] 1:3. In view of the specific order dated 10th July, 1988 which stated that the first order of appointment issued in 1972 shall be continued for a period of one year w.e.f. 30th September 1985 and not from 30th 8 1985, the respondent is entitled to the salary and allowances due to him till 30th October, 1985 if the order was found to be an invalid one.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not reliable, and that the discrepancies in the evidence were of a minor character and that they had been unduly magnified by the Sessions Judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The discrepancies were in regard to which of them woke up first, where was the lantern and which of the neighbours came first to the scene on hearing their cries. The prosecution witnesses were unable to identify the accused making a gesture as if they were stabbing the deceased. [368E F] 2. The discrepancy was not such that it could have been explained by the prosecution. The evidence of P. Ws. 1, 2 and 3 was corroborated by the evidence on record. [369F G] 3. The circumstances relied upon by the High Court had no reasonable relation to the guilt of the appellant or the evidence given by him. The injury was inflicted with great force and its direction was upward. The location of the injury was 6 cms below the arm pit on the left side. According to the prosecution, the deceased received a stab injury. The deceased intervened and interposed herself between P.W. 1 and himself. He regained consciousness next morning. The doctor who examined him found several abrasions and contusions on his person. There was no fracture. There were a minor girl aged about 18 miles from the house of the accused. The medical evidence showed that it was more probable that the deceased was stabbed when she was lying down. [367E F; 368A] 4. The conduct of the witnesses was unnatural and they could not be upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. He probably attributed the refusal to reluctance on the part of his wife to accompany him straightaway. [370B C] 5. The absence of P W. 3, an old woman of 69 years, stated in her evidence that she saw the accused going away from the scene of occurrence and that he had seen the stabbing. He did not state before the High court as to how the injuries could be received in the circumstances mentioned by the accused.[370E F ] 6. The explanation given by P. W.3 that the victim could have received the injury if she was standing, is more probable than that against him. [371F] 7. The fact that the doctor stated that the injury could not have been received in a manner suggested by the defence that is, when the deceased died was lying on her right side. It is true that the accused did not have any deep motive to kill the deceased but he must have been upset by persistent refusal to send the finger prints of the victim to his near relations. He perhaps attributed the failure to reluctance to reluctance. [372F G; 371A] 8. The injuries were inflicted with considerable force and their direction was rational. The place of occurrence was not aiscrepant, free possibility in the instant case, and the evidence was insufficient to establish that the incident took place at about 10 p.m. The witnesses were not reliable. [373B C; 371E] 9. The delay in lodging the F.I.R. and the delay in recording the Fard, which is fatal, has been explained away by the fact that P.Ws. 1 to 3 did not disclose the name of the assailant. The Doctor who examined them in the hospital in the first instance, stated that he was stabbed only when she fell down. The trial court held that the prosecution had failed to establish motive and that it had not been proved that the injuries were caused in the manner suggested. [374B C, D] 10. The incident took a possible view and acquitted the accused on the basis of the statement of P,W. 3.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as a Judge in the Supreme court by warrant under section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was later transferred to the High Court and then to another Court. The President of India promulgated an ordinance called the Prevention and Control of Corruption (Amendment) Ordinance, 1978 which came into force on October 30, 1978. In the meantime, the appellant, who was a Judge, was removed from his office by an order dated December 31, 1978 passed under section 5(1) (c) read with article 124(4) of Constitution of India. The appellant challenged the validity of the ordinance in a writ petition before the High court which dismissed it on the ground that it was not applicable to him as he was not given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the Judges of the High Courts or of the high Court from his duties as a judge. The High Court also held that the President had no authority to remove such a Judge as required by section 6 (1)(C) of Act, and that the competent authority to appoint and to remove him from his post was not the Chief Justice of the Andhra Pradesh High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the power to punish a Judge under section 4(1), (c), (d) and (e) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act, could be exercised only by the President and not by the Governor General in case of a Judge or Chief Justice. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of clause (e), (f) and clause (5) of Article 124 read with Article 4(4), and (5)(5) are clear on the point that Section 6(i)(c), specifically enjoins that their position would be akin to that of a Chief Justice and the Supreme Courts have no legal sanction behind it making it justiciable. [255B] 2. The word "office" in clause (c ) of sub section (1) of Section 5, is used in the widest sense to include Judges of High Court, as well as Judges of a High Court; and for this reason, the expression "any other person" in the clause cannot be restricted to the Chief justice of India, but only because such a person is not a vertical superior. [256C D] 3. The words "in the case of any person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union and is not removable from his Office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government" are clear enough to confer on the President the power of appointing and dismissing a Judge other than the Chief Judicial Magistrate, and for that reason such constitutional functionaries do not fall within the purview of the Act. [257D] 4. The expression "in any case" in Clause (e ) has to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of competent authority under Section 6 of the . [257E] 5. The ambit of the enactment is to be determined on the basis of the public office held by the public serv ice, which office is alleged to have been abused during the tenure for committing the offence of criminal misconduct under the Act and it is not the fact of continuance in that office or ceasing to hold it which decides the ambit of Section 6. [258G H] 6. The purpose of the legislation is to provide a speedy remedy to the aggrieved person against a Judge who may be found guilty of criminal charge, as a result of which he has been deprived from his official duties and his trial is not contemplated by Section 6 (i)(e) or (ii). [258H; 259A] 7.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were the members of the Sitya Saha caste specified in item 40 of Part 13 of the Schedule to the Order which set out the Scheduled Castes which were declared Sche duled castes. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on various grounds, but the High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant belonged to a smaller caste group within the bigger caste group and did not belong to the Schedule Caste specified in Item 40. HELD: (i) The Tribunal rightly held that the respondent belonged to the smaller caste Group of Sahas. [390 B] (ii) The order passed by the High court was correct. When the item excluded Sahas from Sunri caste, those who bore the surname Saha must equally be another caste group. The Tribunal thought that the Sahas were originally a smaller Caste group within its Sunri category and they had been specifically excluded in item40 for greater safety o prevent them from claiming to be Sunris by reason of their origin. [391 C] (iii) The appellant was not entitled to succeed on the ground that he belonged to an independent caste which had nothing to do with the Sun name Saha. He must be held to belong to a Scheduled Caste specified under item 40. That being so, the election petition must fail. [392 D E] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that the Tribunal 's finding that the Sitia excluded were those Sunri by their surname, whatever might be their other characteristics, was altogether irrelevant to the point in issue. Evidence cannot alter the natural interpretation of the words in the Order.

The appellant was convicted under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellant demanded a sum of Rs. 30,000 as rent from the respondent for occupying the premises as caretaker. The appellant pleaded that he had been in possession of the premises on 4 12 1948 and that he was in fact to be a caretder of his flat and that the money was paid by him to the complainant 's brother who was the second respondent in this appeal. The defence of the appellant was that he took with him Rs. 29,500 as rent for the furniture and that on the date of the delivery of the possession he had no claim whatsoever over this amount. Held, that the prosecution under section 19(2) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, LVII of 1947 was not barred by article 134(1)(c) of Constitution. The word "relinquishment" in section 19 of the Act does not occur in the Transfer of Property Act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are sections which deal with the relinquishment of their holdings by tenants in favour of the landlord by notice given to him in writing. The section in question, therefore, does not speak of relinquishment or giving up of possession,in general terms. In the present case, the respondent was not in possession on 412 1948 and he had only been to act as cares for himself.

The appellant company was a partnership firm. It was dissolved and in 1974 the undertaking became one of the divisions of Tata Sons Limited. The Company was dissolved on December 22, 1978. In 1974 the Company made a reference to the Industrial Tribunal under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal took note of the fact that besides the staff of workmen represented by the Union there were several other employees who would also have to be paid dearness allowance in addition to the benefits conferred by the revised pay scales and other awarded reliefs. The award was made on December 20, 1978 and an application under Rule 31 of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957 was filed before the Tribunal for a correction of an error apparent on the face of the record. The application was opposed by the appellant company contending that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible to bear the additional financial burden. The Industrial Tribunal took into account the fact of financial capacity of the appellant, the Tribunal held that the Company was in an undoubted position to bear additional financial liability and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of basic wage. It also observed that the Tribunal had not taken into account any industrial dispute which would have imposed an unreasonable restriction on the appellant 's right to claim the cost of living index and that the additional dearness allowance was being granted by the company at 10% of the salary subject to a minimum of Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories. The High Court dismissed the application for correcting the award. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that having regard to the financial capacity, the tribunal erred in making the wage scales retrospective and in any event in ranging from Rs. 150/ to Rs. 200/ per month. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The basic question considered by the Industrial Court is the question of revision of the wage structure.

The respondent, an award holder of a Sugar Factory, was awarded wages for two days and in pursuance thereof the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award. This agreement was subsequently published in the Bihar Gazette as a part of the award, and in spite of the Award and the agreement, the appellant paid its employees only As. /10/ per day and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appel lant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the respondents the said prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas, one that section 15 was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the Award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. The authority held that section 2 (vi) includes wages fixed under the award but that the claims of the respondent were barred by time. The Authority held that the applications made by respondents were competent under section 25 of the Industrial Disputes Act before the Patna High Court and dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The authority did not decide the said question as a preliminary question because it held, and, in view of the definition prescribed by s 2(iv) of the , that the wages prescribed were not payable under section 2.(vi), the wage structures prescribed by an award could not fall under the definition provided by section2(vi). [417 D E] The authority had found that section was applicable to the case because the wages fixed in the award did amount to wages as defined by section 25. Therefore, the application of the provisions of the Indus trial Disputes Act was barred.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department of Pepsu. He was charged under section 409, Indian Penal Code for having dishonestly removed certain medicines from a hospital which he had taken from a doctor to his residence and thereby committed an offence under section 120 B of the Indian Penal code. The trial court convicted him but the High Court acquitted him on the ground that the prosecution had failed to establish that the amount drawn by him did not reach the hands of the appellant as required by section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the conviction was illegal and the absence of sanction under section 197 (1) Of the Code was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The mere fact that the entrustment and/or dominion were in an official capacity, did not affect the maintainability, as the entrustment or dominion was a matter of defence on the merits, which would have to be determined by the trial court, and could not arise at the stage of granting sanction under s 197(i) Of Cr. P.C., [1948] L.R. 75 I.A. 185, relied on. The fact that entrustment and dominion were not in an office or a public servant was immaterial because the entrustment was in an officer 's capacity and it was equally evident that there could be no disposal, lawful or otherwise, save by an act done or purporting to be done in an Official capacity. The question whether sanction is necessary for prosecuting a public Servant must depend on the facts of each case. In the present case, the appellant received the sum of Rs. 51 alleged to have been misappropriated and was subsequently transferred to his place of residence and he admitted receipt of it.

The assessee was a banking company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State. The income tax authorities included only the profit which was allowed to be set off against profits and gains under section 24(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee contended that the business losses incurred by him could not be set apart against profits made in Travancore State as they were not received or brought into British India within British India. Held, that the proviso to section 24 (1) Of the Indian Incometax Act, did not apply to the year of assessment and that the loss was not set off under section 4(3). The assessee could claim a deduction of the losses incurred in Travancore state only if it had carried on business in British India or in the case of Travancore State. It was not necessary for the assessee to obtain any such permission as he might have obtained the right of adjustment on account of his share of loss in the firm, whether the set off be against other profits under section 9(3) Of Act. The proviso could apply only where the loss sustained is a loss of profits or gains and not where there was no positive words which would support an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head " business ". Held, further, that to say that business in section 10 means business in India or business the profits or losses of which are taxable in British Indian State is to ignore the definitions and sections 3, 4 and 6. The mere use of the words loss of profit or gains to be, set offagainst profits and gain would not be sufficient to restrict the scope of the proviso.

The appellant company was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co., which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. In July 1947, the Private Limited company was converted into a Public Limited Company. The Head Office of the Company is at Calcutta. It has branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via Madras. The General practice of the company both at the Head Office and the Branch offices appears to have been to retire at the age of 55 though in certain cases the company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age Of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the ageof 55. The Company 's employees at Bombay raised a dispute regarding their retirement age. They claimed that no workman should be retired from service before he bad completed 60 years of age. The Tribunal held that the age was fixed at 60 and the company could in its option, after he attained the age prescribed by the agreement for 58 years, apply for an medical examination to the interests of the employers and what is even more important to the general interest of the country at large industrial adjudication had to pay special attention to the prevailing practice in the industrial region concerned. The High Court on appeal held that though the Tribunal had found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region, the trend had been to fix the retirement age at 60, it was not challenged before this Court by the workmen. Held: (i) The Tribunal has rightly rejected the Company ' s claim for fixing the age at 58 years. The approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very commendable and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was in fact inaccurate. (ii)The Tribunal has failed to notice that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an already decided case about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. The awards and agreements on the question of age of retirement about which information is furnished by the several documents on this record clearly show a consistent trend in the Bombay region to fix retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60. (iii)The award of the Tribunal has not been challenged before the Supreme Court.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1961 and its incorporation in the year 1961. The Board of Directors of the company passed a resolution on May 19, 1965 to sell its assets to M/s. Mitchell Ltd., for Rs. 1,00,000/ . The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order of the Board dated May 19. 1965 and also sought directions from the Board to restrain it from giving effect to the order dated May 9, 1965. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Board had acted on material extraneous to the matters mentioned in section 237(b) of the Act and that the order was invalid because it was made by the Chairman of the board and not by the Board. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 (b) is merely administrative and not judicial. It is difficult to appreciate how the allocation of business of the respondent company relating to the exercise of such power can be anything other than a matter of procedure. For sub section (6) of section 10E it is incumbent upon the Board of directors to make a report to the Central government which, in the opinion of the Chairman, has not been satisfactory or that the affairs of the Company have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members. The power is conferred on them by section 10 E(5) only when there are circumstances suggesting that fraud, collusion or misconduct may be committed in relation to the company 's affairs. [334 C D] (ii) The Board has been constituted under section 237 and the powers are exercised with the permission of the Central Govt. In exercise of its power under section 235(b), the Chairman acts as a delegatee. It cannot therefore be said that the power conferred by section 9(6) is administrative.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced it to one under section 411 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence strengthens the other evidence already against him. [724 D] (ii) If the gap of time is too large, the presumption that the accused was concerned with the murder would have been drawn. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case. It all depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime are made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap is too small, the finding must be under section 41 1 of the Evidence Act, 1872. [700 E F] (iii) The time gap in some cases is as short as two days and in some others it is not more than five days. In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be drawn. they need not he stated here. It would depend upon the circumstance under which discovery of fruits of the crime are make with a Particular accused. [624 F G] (iv) The sentence is reduced to three years rigorous imprison ment.

The petitioners, who were carrying on business in poisons, challenged the constitutional validity of Section 5 of the , as amended by the Delhi Po lice (Amendment) Act, 1973. The High Court dismissed their writ petition holding that section 5 of Act 1 of 1963 was not applicable to them and that the restriction imposed on possession for sale and sale were not reasonable restrictions. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 2(3) of the Act impliedly sets out certain guidelines when the State can notify a substance as poison. It states that the State Government may by rule regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons. Some substances which the Govern ment consider its possession for Sale or sale to be regulated in the interest of health and safety of the society. This limitation is inherent in the scheme of the . Act itself. Of course no comprehensive definition can be given to the word poison. Under this term would fall anything calcu lated to destroy life. Substances harmless in themselves might become poison by the time or manner of their adminis tration. [223E F] 1.2 The provisions of neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. The petitioners have also taken the plea that though the Act is a Central enactment it is possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory appli cation as it is left to each State Government to determine what substance they would include as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale, and sale or sale of the same. It is in exercise of this power Rule 13 was amended by adding a guideline. [222B C] 1:3. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as an poison for purpose of the Central Act. Rules were amended in 1973 and duly notified as required by the Act. Section 2 (3) enables the State Govern ment to make rules generally to carry out the purposes and objects of the, Act. Rule 13 is not hit by anyone. [220D E] 1 :4.

The appellant firm was carrying on business of import and export of yarn. The profits for the assessment year 1952 53 were disallowed by the Income tax Officer, but in appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner agreed with the Income Tax Officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended that the debt in question was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the appellant; and that the finding of the Tribunal was very brief and that it gave no reasons in support of its conclusions. The Tribunal rejected this contention. On a reference being made at the instance of the Revenue, the High Court held that the Tribunal had wrongly disallowed the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off by the assessee in their books of account as irrecoverable. In appeal to this Court it was urged on behalf of the assessee that the debts were due in respect of loans made in the ordinary course of business of appellants and therefore the Tribunal erred in disallowing a sum of Rs 2, 68,385 written off. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the sums in question were not sent to the Bombay firm as loans made by the appellant in the normal course of its money lending. [419 D] (i) The finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal is binding on this Court and it cannot be denied that the findings reached by the tribunal are findings of fact and those findings are supported by the evidence on record. [420 E F] (ii) The Tribunal after catalogueing the arguments advanced at the bar, has come to certain abrupt conclusions but all the tame it cannot now be denied the finding reached by this Court. It is true as contended by the Revenue that the conclusions reached by it were not supported by proper discussion of the material before it. It was also true that the tribunal after catalyogueing its arguments advanced in the bar has come into certain abreasts but all these facts are supported only by proper consideration of the evidence adduced before it and cannot be relied upon. [416 G H] (iii) The conclusion reached by Tribunal is not supported either by proper reasoning or proper discussion. It can be denied even if it is not in respect Of loan, but a debt due in the usual course of his money lending, business or the assessee.

The petitioners challenged the acquisition of certain lands in question by the respondents under the provisions of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. The High Court granted interim stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that as the awards in these cases had not been made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed and that since the awards were not made within one year from September 20, 1984, the whole acquisition proceedings was lapsed. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave Petitions. [565F] 2. The facts of the case are highly material and there is no reference in the special leave petitions to any to the stay order and it is beyond dispute that the fact of stay orders were highly material. [566D] 3. The petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in the Special Leave Petition pending before the High Court, till September 20. 1985. [567F G] 4. Whatever the ultimate effect of the staying orders was very material in that case only when the respondents appeared in response to the notice and filed their counter affidavit. In the instant case, the said interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. [568F G; 566G] 5. The Special Leave petitions are dismissed.

The appellant bank claimed that under cl. (ii) of the Sastry Award, the adjusted basic pay in the new scale was not to exceed what point adjustment would give to an employee more than the maximum in the old scale. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the adjustment was justified and directed the appellant bank to compute the benefit to which they were entitled under the Sastry award as they were not satisfied with the fixation of their pay by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The adjustment basic pay has to be worked out as on January 1, 1959, the two increments provided by cl. The workman 's basic pay as on 1st January, 1959 cannot be reduced and therefore when cl. is read in the light of cl. 5(a), it must refer to the same date as in cl. [905 D E] (ii). The adjustment in the present case was not a matter of fixation of pay but was subject to cl. Therefore, cl. 3(b) is subject to cls. (i), (ii), and (iii). [904 F G] Prakash Chand Mehra vs C.A. 1008 and Bharat Chand Mehra 's case, ; , followed. (iii) The appellant bank 's contention that the words "subject to rules" in cl.(iv) of para 5(b), namely, for changes necessitated by the fact that the Desai award was being given in 1962 and (iv) the adjustment basic salary as on February 1, 1962, could not be allowed to be deducted under sub cls. 2 and 3 of cl, 5(i).

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, had maintained an account in the books of M/s. Pearls & Beads and it did not have any overdraft facilities with any bank. The assessee had a cash balance of Rs.4,299 but it did have no overdraft facility with any Bank. The Income Tax Officer held that there was no valid gifts of Rs,67,560 to the assessee and therefore the amounts were rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In reference the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in answering the question against the assessee on the facts of the case. [130D] 1.2 The High court was in a position to hold that the assessee had made a valid gift of Rs 50,000 to his son and to his wife, K, by making debit entries in the account books of the firm and corresponding credits to the accounts of L and K. [131E F] 1:3. In the instant case, each case must be decided on the circumstances of that case. Where the assessee has a credit amount with firm or with family or with a banking company and that sum is available to that firm or the company or H.U.F. on the date of the gift, then a valid gifts by book entries might be possible but where a sum was not available with the firm or family or a company which was not a banking Company or which had no overdraft facilities, by mere book entries even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid transfer. [132F G] 1 :4. The High COurt was in wrong in answering a question in the manner it did. [133G] 1 5. In order to decide whether there was a valid gifted amount or trust in respect of the said amounts, the High court must consider the effect of the two decisions of the Allahabad High Court and the Madras High Court on the point. The order and judgment of the High COrt are set aside. [134A] 1 6. In view of the decision of the Division Bench of the Delhi High Court in C.I.T., Punjab, Haryana, J. & K. (judgment by one of us) had to deal with the wealth tax liability of the respondent and the High Courts were right in answering it against the Revenue on the ground that the question was not rightly decided. [135E] 7. The orders and judgment are set at naught.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 were framed by the State Government under article 235(b) of the Constitution. Under Rule 3(1)(a) of that Rules the High Court was empowered to appoint a person or persons as a judge or to one of the posts in the secretariat. The High Court held that the power to appoint the Registrar of the High Courts was exclusively vested in the Chief Justice and not with the Governor. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had no authority to hold the posts and that the transfer of the District Judges already appointed or promoted and posted in the cadre was in violation of article 235 of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The power to transfer judges is included in the control vested in it by article 235 as the control given to the High courts over the district courts under that Article includes control over the officers who preside over those courts. [161 F] (2) The executive cannot know the requirements of a particular court, the High Commissioner being the head of the department, he has to follow the rules laid down in that decision. He is not expected to act as a custodian of the control over district courts. It is not the case of the parties that he was placed at the disposal of the Government for any definite period. [162 B C] (3) The High Courts have power to issue directions to the State Governments and not to interfere with their functions. [163 E F] In the instant case, the cadre of the superior judicial service consisted of not only the posts of district and sessions judges but also officers holding other posts. One of the officers included there was the Registrar, of the Assam High Court and the Judicial remembrance and the member sales tax tribunal respectively. The cadre of a superior judicial officer consisted of three parts i.e., (1 ) presiding officers of district courts, (2), the Registrar and (3). (4) the senior most judicial officer in grade II. The posts of the law secretary, deputy law Secretary and other legal remembrancer were included in that cadre. [164 E F; 164 A B] (5) The cadre was not a single cadre consisting of officers under the direct control of the high office department. It consisted of the Registrar who was then functioning to the cadre. No doubt all these officers belong to the judicial service of the State and they were before 1962 presiding over district Courts or courts subordinate to them and as such were under the control of High Court. [165 E F, H] (6) The Government had already implemented that part of the order as well. Those officers are now functioning in the posts to which they were transferred. The learned Attorney General was not prepared to accept the contention that the Government had no power to hold these posts. [166 G H; 167 A B].

The appellant purchased certain agricultural land and village immovable property from the vendor respondent No. 1. The sale deed was executed on May 2, 1960 by the mother of the vendor. The mother died in 1963. The widow of the vendors filed a suit for partition of the said land. The appellant contended that she fell within the expression other co sharers ' in clause (1) of section 15(1)(b) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 and as such entitled to pre empt the right of pre emption under clause (fourthly), of section15(1) (b). The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that there was no infringement of Article 19(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharer and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharists jointly, the remaining part of section fifteen(1), (thirdly) and (third) of Section 15( 1)(b), were not hit by Article 19 (1). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The purport of the Court 's decision in Attam Prakash 's case was to deny the right to those relative or relatives of the owner or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section 5(1 ) (b) even if they happen to be co shariers. [127F] 1.2 The intention of the legislature was to confer the right on specified family members of the vendee or vendors in the first three clause which was meant to serve as a residuary clause to ensure that no co shar er was left out or omitted and not to deny, the right for kin to kinstolkars covered by the preceding clauses. If the preceding clause were not erased from the statute book as unconstitu tional the kinsfolk would have exercised the right in the order of preference, for which no justification was found. The relations in the second three clauses could not be challenged on the ground that they happened to be cooperative class by themselves. [128B C] 1:3. In the instant case, the appellant is seeking to exercise the right conferred on him under clause 4 (fourth) of Punjab Preemption Act, 1914, prior to its amendment in 1960.

The appellants and the respondents were the sons of one S.A.R. The father of S. A.R died in 1985 leaving a son S.B.R., S.N.R, and his wife S.L.P. Nos. 12288 of 1984 were brought on record as legal representatives. The appellants filed an application for partition of the entire property claiming that they had become owners of the property by virtue of sale deeds executed in their favour by S.D.R in 1985. The respondents contested the suit and contended that S.S.A was not entitled to receive Rs. 1 lakh more than Rs.1 lakh as stipulated under the deeds. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had not been paid Rs. I lakh as per the deeds of sale and that S would deliver vacant possession of the properties by 30th April, 1991. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the alienees had no interest in the property prior to the compromise for which there is no acceptable evidence. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The alienation are pendente lite. [541C] 2.1 The alienees have no interest therein. Their possession is without authority of law. Ordinarily, they would have been liable to account for mesne profits. In view of the fact that there was the allegation of payment of Rs.l lakh to S.K. which we have not investigated and to meet the further allegation that some improvements have been made to the property which too we have no direct interest in it. [542F G] 2:2 The alienee has no interest created under the alleged sale deeds. Their posses sion is without any authority of Law. Ordinarily they would be liable to accounts for mesne profit. In a suit for title and injunction, the Court can only record the same and no option lay before the court to act otherwise. [543F G; 543A] 2 :3 The alienors have no right created under a alleged sale deed. Their Possession is without authori ty of law, and therefore cannot be dis puted. [544B] Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr. vs Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Ori. 108, referred to.

The workers of the appellant company, who were working as absentee employees in its factory, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award of the Industrial Tribunal. The High Court held that the workmen were entitled to 7 days sick leave with full pay and dearness allowance from January 1, 1975 to December 14, 1969 and they were quite adequate, the proper authority to examine the demand for sick leave was the appellant 's employer. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as the benefits granted by the Tribunal were not similar to those admissible under the Industrial Disputes Act, the workmen would be entitled to seven days sick Leave with wages on full pay on the ground of sickness. HELD: The scheme of the benefits admissible under section 49 of the Act cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for leave to the extent allowed by the tribunal. Section 61 of the , provides that a person qualified to claim sickness benefit shall not be entitled, except in the case of a spell of sickness following at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of illness for which the sickness benefit was last paid. It is apparent from section 61 of that Act that the benefits are granted by it only in cases where the workman is entitled to any of the benefit provided by the Act, he shall not otherwise be entitled for the initial waiting period of two days except in cases of continuous illness following at a interval of more than fifteen days, and the spell out of not less than 15 clear days, that amount is not admissible for the first two days of sickness except in case of continuous sickness following. at an intervals of not exceeding 15 days. The Act does not in fact deal with the question of sickness leave. [83 E F] In the instant case, the Tribunal was justified in granting the benefit to the workmen on the basis of the recommendations made by the Industrial Tribunals.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the , with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security of India and to the relations of India with the Portuguese Government. The grounds were served on him along with the order of detention. He challenged his detention by means of a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The right to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest cannot be required. It is not possible to imply any such obligation under article 21 but want of bona fides on the part of the detaining authority. [387 G H] (ii)The question as to whether the grounds furnished are vague or not, is a circumstance which may well be taken into consideration in deciding whether the ground can be considered to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue feeling the grounds to be vague, ask for particulars. An obligation to communicated the decision not to disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest may well he implied in such a situation. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have prejudice the constitutional right. [388 C D] (iii)The failure to furnish particulars and the duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interests are vested in the detaining authori ty, not in any other. It was therefore necessary for the detaining au thority to have furnished particulars and to afford the detenu reasonable opportunity to make a representation.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre. He was charged with having committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegation against him was that he committed acts in contravention of r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. The Central Government directed removal from service of the respondent. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal on the ground that r.14 of the Defence Rules, which was ultra vires the , was ultra rites the . The High Court held that r 14 was ultra vides the Act and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the provisions of the Rules were ultra vires as they had been framed in exercise of the powers conferred by section 191 of the ; (ii) the words "subject to the provisions Of the Act" occurring in section 19 make section 19 subject to the provision of the Act, and such rules, the Central Government may dismiss or remove from service any person subject to this Act. HELD : The words " subject to his Act" in section 191(2)(a) specifically give power to make a rule providing for the removal from the service of persons subject to that Act. It follows that there may be a valid rule where under, subject to other provisions of .the Act, the central Government may remove a person from the Service. [451 B] (iii) The words 'subject to this section ' occurring in s.19 make section 197 subject to section 45 and the Central Govern ment has thus no power to remove a persons from the serv ice in derogation of the provisions. But the power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words ' subject to its provisions ' it speaks of removal of a person ' from the ' service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned.

The appellant was a Panchayat Samiti under the C.P. and Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. The respondent filed an appeal against the order of assessment to octroi duty. The appellant contended that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r. 21, that the appellant should have been importing tea within the limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale and that the Government had no jurisdiction to decide the appeal on merits as the appeal to the Panchayat Samiti was barred by limitation because r. 5 of the Rules framed under section 50 of the Act provided that the procedure prescribed in rr. 3 and 4 should be followed before levying tax. The High Court held that the octroi duty was validly levied and that it could be imposed and collected with effect from January 14, 1964. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 5 must be read along with r.21 and if so read it would mean that before the octroi is approved octroi can be collected. [217 B] (ii) The fixing of the octroi limit with the sanction of the Government is an essential condition precedent to the levy of octroi duty.[218 E] (iii) Rule 3(b) does not require the Panchayat, to fix the octroi area in the resolution passed under r,3(a). The rule requires that the Panchayat should follow the procedure laid down in rr 3 and 7 before levying a tax on buildings and lands. [218 G] (iv) The scheme of the fees Rules is that the general procedure for levying taxes or fees is laid down and then this procedure is made applicable to the imposition of various taxes mentioned in the other parts of the rules.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1), of the , for having committed an offence punishable with imprisonment for a period which may extend to six months or with fine or with both. The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings could be prolonged much beyond what was contemplated by the Act and the termination of the conciliation proceeding was illegal. Held, that the provisions of section 12(6) of the Act were not applicable to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. Section 12(1)(a) provides for commencement and conclusion of conciliation proceedings under section 20 but the first sub section is as follows: " (2) The report of the Conciliation Officer shall be final and conclusive evidence of the fact that the industrial dispute has been pending before a conciliation officer or a Board or of any proceeding before a Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal in respect of an industrial dispute, and such report shall not be deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached. The provisions of sub section 2 apply to all Conciliation proceedings whether under the Act or otherwise". Workers of the Industry Colliery Colliery, Dhanbad vs Management of the industry Colliery, and The State of Bihar vs Management, of the Institution of Labour, [1952] S.C.R. 889, referred to. Held further, that in view of the provisions Of section 12 (6) Of the , the conciliation officer was bound to make his report within 14 days of the commencement of the proceedings or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. Colliery Mazdoor Congress, Asansol vs New Beerbhoom Coal Co., Ltd., ; and Workers of The Industry Colliery, M. P. vs Management Of the Industry, Colliery, (1868) L.R . 7 I.A.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the , by an order dated 2nd January, 1986 passed by the respondent No. 1 under section 3(2) of the . The grounds of detention stated that on 24th December, 1985 between 10 and 1030 A.M., the subject and his associates opened fire at police party which caused serious head injury and was still incapable to work. Charge sheet No. 20/85 was submitted against him in respect of a criminal case under section 307 I.P.C. The petitioner 's representation dated 22nd January 1986 and the petition for bail were rejected by the State Government on the ground that he was produced before the Advisory Board but he was not given any hearing. By letter dated 22th February, 1986 the petitioner was informed that the Advisory board had confirmed the order of detention. The grounds stated that there was indiscriminate firing on 24 December 1985 on Katras Coal Dump and the petitioner started indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendestine business of coal to establish his criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers customers and passers by of the area. The incidents alleged were that the petitioner along with others opened fire on police party, who went to apprehend the petitioner and assaulted him in presence of customers and others. On the question whether the detention order was justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order of preventive detention when it was passed was not invalid and on relevant considerations, the service of the order Was not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the affidavit filed by the District Magistrate though there were indications that transfer of the detenu from one prison to another was considered but the need to serve the detention Order while he was in custody was not properly considered by the detaining authori ty in the light of the relevant factors. At least the records of the case do not indicate that. If that is the position, then however disreputable the antecedents of a person might have been without consideration of all the aforesaid relevant factors, the detenu could not have been put into preventive custody. Therefore, though the order may be invalid and if on relevant consideration it was not proper to detain the authority in the present case properly and seriously before the service. [910C D] 2. The detention order is set aside. The writ petition and the appeal are allowed.

The appellant firm was manufacturing shroffs and dealers in gold. The goldsmiths manufactured by the firm were manufacturers, shroff and dealers. The appellant firm had issued a notification under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 to the effect that the Administrator should have regard to the policy and purposes of the Act in making his orders. The Administrator as is evident from the provision of sec. 28 of Act, 1969 has not been able to effectively combat the smuggling over the long borders and coast line, that therefore anti smuggling measures had to be supplemented by a detailed system of control over internal transactions and that the Gold (Control) Act, 196l, 1968 was passed for this purpose. The High Court struck down sec.28 of the gold Control Act as it stood prior to its amendment by the Amending Act No. 26 of 1969, constitutionally invalid on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been expressly indicated in sec.27 by reference to which the power conferred upon him under sec.29 is not premitted. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The objective, the policy, and the scheme of the enactment together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the , shall not be premitted.[955E] 1.2 In the instant case, the objective, namely, the Policy and the Scheme of the Income Tax Act together with its necessity to ensuring prevention of circumstances in which the permission can be granted or refused, should be upheld by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised power has been conferred upon the Administrator under secs.28(6) of the Wealth Tax Act, and that is not decisive of the matter. [955G H; 956A] 1:3. The objective is the policy of the enact ment and the schemes affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. The main object in putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of the production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. " [956C D] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona, ; , followed. 1:4. The object and the Schemes of the Land Ceiling Act together including the necessity for ensuring prevention and circumvention Of the other provision of the . shall not he premitted, and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a superior authority. [953E] Harkchand Ratan Chand Banthi vs Asst Collector of Customs, ; and Ramanlal Purshottamamdas Chokshi vs Union of India & Ors., , referred to.

The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple in Madras, filed an application under section 87 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, for possession of certain properties belonging to the temple. The trial Court held that the grant was not in favour of the predecessor of the temple but by persons who claimed to be the members of the family as their separate secular properties, though burdened with an obligation to render service to the Matam; and that the appellants had acquired title by adverse possession. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and held that it was not a grant in favour Of the religious endowment within the meaning of article 134 B of the Indian Limitation Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question as to whether the facts proved in the present case did not show that the alienor disposed of all the property and left the village for more than 25 years after effecting the transfer was irrelevant for the purpose of article 133 B. [123 E] Gnanasambanda vs N. R. Tatachari, ; , referred to. (ii) The suit had been brought against respondents 1 to 3 who were appointed trustees of the Temple by respondent No. 4 and their father. The appellants were appointed as trustees of that temple by respondent Nos. 1 to 4. Respondent No. 5 was appointed as a trustee of the trust to take effect from the date on which the alienee was appointed. [124 E] (iii) The fact that the alienation made in favour the appellants was made by persons other than the members who were in management of the properties de facto, did not affect the application of article 135 B. If the transfer is made on the other basis that it belongs to the religious endowments, article 134B would apply; but does not make any difference to the application Of article 134 A. [125 G H] (iv) The title of the respondent No 1 to the property had not been lost by adverse posses sion before the suit was filed. It is only when article 144 B applies that it will be necessary for him also to show that he has been removed more than 12 years before the institution of the suit. [126 C D] (v) The appellants ' case that they were removed from management of a Hindu temple de facto by respondent 1, was not proved by evidence and the lower appellate Court was right in decreeing them.

The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by the District Magistrate and the appellate authority, namely, the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the licence granted to the respondent was for exhibition of cinematograph films in the cinema theatre and that it had become impossible for him to operate the Cinema licence in view of the temporary injunction issued by the Civil Judge, Jammu & Kashmir, restraining the appellant from interfering with the running of the cinema by the respondents. The appellant filed the present appeal after obtaining special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by District Magistrate directing the suspension of the licence is not one suspending the licence issued in respect of the Theatre. What was done thereunder was to suspend the exhibition cinematograph films. [582B] 2. The impugned order is one obviously passed by a District Magistrate in the exercise of his function of administering the provision of the Act and the Rules and the implied power to take all incidental steps necessary for effective enforcement of the statute. [593C D] 3. The writ petitioners could not have any legitimate expectation that they will be allowed to run the Theatre without a licence in violation of the law. [592F] 4. The District Magistrate had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned order. It is well settled that under the Act the power to suspend a licence is conferred only by section 6 F of the , as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the said section are present, the licensing authority had no juris diction to suspend or revoke the license. [591D E] 5. The power to control the exhibition of the cinematograph films is vested solely in Ved Gupta, the licensee. It cannot be said that he has any right or legitimate expectation from the person other than the licensee or his authorised representative. [589F G] 6. The State Government had no power under the , to suspend an licence unless it was found that the licensee had been expelled from the partnership. [590G H] 7. The licensing authority has no jurisdiction in the matter of granting a license to run a cinema without a license in contravention of the provisions of the . [591A B] 8. The right to conduct the exhibition is vested exclusively in Ved Prakash, the licencee. It can only be done by an elected representative. The licence cannot be revoked merely because it was granted for the purpose of running the cinema. [588E F] 9. The license granted by the licensing authori ty in favour of Ved Prakash in his individual capacity and he alone was the licensee, is a licensee. He has no right whatever to conduct or continue in law to conduct such exhibition of films. There was no suspension of licence issued to Ved Prakash. [587F G; 588A] 10.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 they entered into an agreement with them for the purchase of the stock of raw materials, unsold finished goods, spare parts, cars etc. The agreement provided that the mills and the factory in question would be sold only to the appellants. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellant under section 7 of the , stating that they had systematically committed breaches of the various terms on which the properties bad been leased to them and called upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and they were accordingly required not to remove the stock or raise any money on the security thereof. The appellants filed a suit for a declaration that the lease granted by him was not void as it had become the property of the respondent and had become vested in the respondent as the Custodian for the State. The trial court held that the notice was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under section 12 of the Act, but on appeal the High Court confirmed the decision. On appeal to this Court by special leave: Held, that the suit was not barred by article 14 Of the Constitution and the appellants were entitled to relief under the provisions of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1950. The notice dated 13 2 1954 issued by the appellants was therefore valid. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, , applied. The operative portion of section 12 which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof is unqualified and absolute and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force".
