Aggrieved by the order of the High court, the appellant filed appeals before this Court. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.

The expression "newspaper" is defined by section 2(b) of the Act as meaning any printed periodical, fortnightly or monthly work containing news. The term `news paper ' is usually applied to newspapers which are not ordinarily used in the ordinary parlance of the highest court of the land. In order to make it a newspaper industry, the Government of India, by an order dated 20th December 1955, published in the Gazette of India and accepted a part of the recommendations made by the Palekar Tribunal. The first respondent, All India Reporter Limited, publishes in addition to the law reports referred to in the first paragraph of this judgment several other books commentaries, digests and manuals. But the first respondent does not send any reply to the questionnaire issued by the Tribunal nor is it informed that the first Respondent has sent a reply to questionnaires in respect of the matters referred to therein. However on 15th July 1981, the Deputy Labour Commissioner, Nagpur wrote a letter to the first and second respondents requesting them to file their written statements in the matter of non implementation of the Pseudars ' working journalists ' and other documents. The 1st respondent also did not send a reply within the time stipulated by the Government order dated 15th August 1981. The Ist respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice served on it by the Deputy Commissioner, and the first respond ents. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the law report published by the Public Analyst was not newspaper within the meaning of section 2 (b) and that the demand made by him was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April 1983. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The law reports published by 1st Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the Ist Respondent in their production or publication of the said law reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Government on the basis of the recommendation made by Paleakar Award.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises. He continued to occupy and use the premises for the purpose of carrying out his business in workshop for a period of five years. The respondent landlord filed an ejectment petition against the appellant under section 41 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 on the ground that he was a tenant of tho suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. The appellant contended that he had been inducted into the premises by the respondent in favour of the appellant as a monthly licensee and that the landlord had failed to prove that he is a sub tenant of him and that he has given workshop to the respondent for conducting business. The trial court passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the appellant against the respondent. The appellate court dismissed the appeal holding that the appellant was not a subtenant as he was not the owner of the workshop and also denied that he ever visited the premises under one Sugrabindo Mohammed Husain who himself had adopted the ejectment proceedings against him. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed before it by the tenant. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the respondent landlord in his written statement had granted a licence in respect of certain shop premises and had produced a rent receipt for the month of April 1971 for a monthly rent of Rs.56; and (ii) the licensee had not created any lease by the document mentioned therein and the appellant regarded him as a mere licensee. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent landlords were in possession of the premises and were machinery belonging to the appellant and not to the tenant.[1066D] 1.2 In view of the fact that the rent light bill stood in the name of the respondent showing that there was no desire to create any lease, by the documents mentioned therein, and the facts and circumstances of this case, it is a licence and not a lease. [1065E F] 1:3 The appellant had been carrying on business for some time and had also produced a copy of the rent receipt showing that the period of licence had come to an end. He was a licensee and not the tenant since he had adopted another round of litigation. The fact that he did not have any equity in favour with regard to the premises would not amount to a lease as such.

The respondent was a Ruler of former princely State in Rajasthan. He applied for the grant of a permit to export his entire quantity of 15,000 maunds of chuni in Madhya Pradesh and in connection therewith he deposited Rs. 30,000 as export duty in advance. The respondent claimed refund of this amount on the ground that it was not extended by any agreement between the former princes and the former State of Dholpur. The State of Rajasthan rejected the claim but the respondent filed a suit for recovery of the amount paid by him. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree holding that the liability of the former Ruler to refund the amount was not contingent on the agreement between him and the old sovereign of the existing rights of the residents of those territories. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the State of Rajas had been bound by the obligation of the new sovereign to pay the refund; (ii) the respondent was not bound by any liability which might have arisen against it under article 295(2); and (iii) even if there was some doubt about the new State undertaking the liabilities of the old States, the new Government could not be held liable under article 294(2). HELD : The new sovereign throughout this process of integration from 1948 to 1950 must be taken to have recognised the rights of subjects and undertaken the liability, if any, of the Old States. It follows that there was recognition of liability by the new state throughout this period and under the circumstances the suit was main tainable against the Part B State of Jaipur. [180 D] (i)(a) The new State recognised the right of the subjects and undertook the liability which may arise against it by virtue of the continuance of the original laws, even if the new States had been merged in the United State of the Rajasthan as it was on January 26, 1950. [181 F G] (b) The change in the old State from 1948 onwards to 1950 cannot be said to have been recognised by the New State at any time and in that respect the present case was not a new sovereign which was an act of State within the meaning of article 295 of the Constitution. [182 B C] (c) The newly formed State of Pepsu had merged into the United States of Rajasthan as a Part B state of Rajasthan under the Covenant entered into by it with the Government of India and there was no recognition of that liability by it. [183 E F] (ii)(a). The new Government throughout this territory had undertaken the liabilities, ifany, of tho old State. It could not therefore be said that the new Part B States assumed the liabilities.

The appellant was a dealer in cotton and groundnut. He had been running the market as an occupation or business with high standards and that he had to take out licences for selling his produce at proper rates. The respondent, who was a manufacturer of commercial crops, applied under section 18 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, for the establishment of a market committee at Virudhunagar and markets at Virudha, for fixing the rates of the members Market Committees. The appellant contended that the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder were not only unreasonable but also violative of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. Held, that the Act was valid and did not contravene articles 14 and 19(i)(f). The Act was an integrated one and it regulates the buying and selling of commercial crop in the State and the Act imposed restrictions on the sale of such commercial crops to the traders. The Act provided for the better regulation of the buying, selling and selling commercial crops by providing for the minimum standard of markets. The provisions of section 5(1) were not violative of articles 19(2)(f), (g) and (g). The provisions relating to the establishment and maintenance of the market established a market which could be established in the manner provided by law. The restrictions imposed by the Act were reasonable and did in any way affect the trade or business of the appellant. The imposition of the restrictions was not unreasonable because the market committee did not name the allowance or allowances taking them out of the provi sions of section 14 of the , which they were entitled to do under that section, but made the bye law mentioning the 'makkal ' allowance as one not deductible in any transaction. The object of the impugned Act was to protect the growers and traders from being subjected to exploitation by them. The fact that the growers may be exempted from payment of sales tax would not make it a trade allowance. The levy of sales taxes on the appellant was not justified under article 19 (1) (f).

The appellant was convicted for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the sentence of death on appeal, but reduced it to life imprisonment. The appellant contended that the conviction should be maintained but was not accepted by the High Court. Held, that the High Courts were right in convicting the appellant under section 302 Indian Penal Code. Section 34 of the Indian Penal code is a special provision and must be read with section 149 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It is well settled that a common intention presupposes prior concert. In a case like that, each would be individually liable for whatever injury he caused but none could be vicariously convicted for the act of any of the others; and if the prosecution cannot prove that his separate blow was a fatal one he cannot be convicted of the murder however clearly an intention to kill could be proved in his case. The circumstances showed that there was no prior meeting of minds to form a pre arranged plan. The fact that the appellant raised their axes and sticks at the assault, did not affect the conclusion of the High court that the common intention was not only to have direct proof of prior concert or proof of circumstances which necessarily lead to that inference, but also that none could he vicariously convicted of an act of murder. The evidence showed that the two accused were responsible for the death of the deceased and the appellant had no motive for the murder. There was no evidence of any prior meeting. The mere fact that there were some other persons could not be used as a motive to kill the deceased, but none would have the common object required by section 34 of Indian Penal Act.

The petitioner was a Sub Inspector of Police in the Central Public Works Department. He was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.76 made under Rule 56(j) of the Fundamental Rules. The vires of Rule 56 (j) was challenged before this Court by the petitioner on the ground that he was holding an officiating appointment in Class II service and, therefore, could not have been compulsorily retired under sub clause (i). This contention was rejected by this Court. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 56 of Fundamental Rules is meant to cover only those who are in a post on a regular basis i.e. in a substantive capacity, and not on an officiating basis only. The possibility of such incumbent being sent back to his substantive post before the power of retirement is exercised, the Government servant con tended must be taken to be in Class I or Class II Service or post at the relevant time and would come within the ambit of sub clause(i). [637C D] 2. Sub clause (ii) of Rule56(j), which applies to Government servants in Class 1 or Class 11 service or post, on substantive, temporary or offi cial or off ence basis, is meant only to those who were in a Post on a substantive basis i,e. In a substantive capaci ty, and cannot be introduced into the scheme. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 is to classify Government servants into two categories and sub clause 1 takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the rele vant time are in Class l or Class III service or posts, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis. [638E F] 3. Sub Clause (i) of rule 56(1) applies to government servants in class I or class II service or Post on substantive. temporary or ficer temporary or on officiated basis. On this conclusion the writ peti tion is liable to be dismissed. [625F G] 4. The petitioner would have superannuated from service on 29.2.1980 if he had not been compulsorily retire ed with effect from 5.11. 1976. Even if the writ is allowed and the order of compulsory retirement is set aside, the petitioner would be entitled to salary and other service allowances payable to him from the date of compulsory retire ment till the date he has been normal superannuation. [737F G; 634A] Tahiliani 's case does not apply to the facts of this case as the petitioner had not attained the age of 55 years by the date when the order was made. The question is whether a Government servant officiating in Class 11 or Class I service or a post even when he held a post of either class III or temporarily or from officiating basis, would be eligible for exercising the power under Rule 57(j)(i) after he has attained the normal age of 50 years. [ 634C D; 634D] Tahilani ' s case does no support the petitioner. But the correct ness thereof is disputed by the Additional Solicitor General appearing for the Union of India and that is why the Court directed that the Union Government will have no objection to treat the petitioner alike and would be prepared to give the same relief to the petitioner.[637E F; 634F] Tahiani ' 's cases do not apply.

The respondent, who was the husband of respondent No. 1, had taken a proposal for insurance for Rs. 50,000 on 27th December 1960. The deceased died intestate on 12th January 1961. The widow of the deceased filed a suit against the appellant Corporation and the Life Insurance Corporation of India for recovery of the amount. The defence of the Corporation was that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the corporation that the payment of first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal and advised the deceased to pay the first premium in full or in part. The appellant Corporation contended that the proposal was not accepted and as such there was no concluded contract. The trial court held that there was a concluded contract, and decreed the suit. On appeal by the Corporation, the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court and held that the policy of the respondent was complete by offer and acceptance and that the other averments in the claim that the appellant was assured were not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to the acceptance of proposal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the Corporation that the Corporation had not filed any evidence of any order prohibiting other officers one step below in rank, in this case the Assistant Divisional Manager of the Life insurance Corporation and on that basis reversing the decision of the Subordinate Judge that the letter of the Divisional Manager was not a concluded valid contract of insurance. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that there is a concluded agreement of insurance between the deceased and local agent. [359E] 2.1 The expression "underwrite" signifies accept liability under '. '. The dictionary meaning also indicates that the expression "Underwrite", signifies accept liaison, or "underwriting". It is true that normally the expression 'underwrites ' signifies acceptation under ' '. But in the instant case, it is clear that the expressions used in Chapter III of the Financial Powers of the Standing Order in this ease specifically used the expression `underwriting and revivals ' of policies in case of Life Insurance Corpora tion and stated that it was the Divisional manager who was competent to underwrite policy for Rs 50, 000 and above. The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death of the applicant or the mere preparation of the policy document is not acceptance. [360F G] 2:2. In the instant cases, the letter written by the Divisional Office to the Divisional office showed that the purpose of review slip was to enable the Divisional officer to assess the risk and take a decision according to the deponent. The letter was issued on behalf of the local authority. It is clear from the letter that the word 'under write ' signifies acceptance and not acceptance, as prima facie acceptance must be communicated to the offeror. [361H; 362A B] 2 :3. The plaintiffs applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter written by them to the Bank. The trial court granted the injunction and the High Court confirmed the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) An order passed by the High court in appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding is not final within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). [707 D] (2) The expression "final order" in section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. An order under section 205 is final within its meaning if it amounts to a final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in the suit or proceedings. If after the order is made, the suit is not to be tried, after the orders are made, but the suit in such a case expressly determines the point in dispute, and brings into the right of the party in dispute to determine the question finally decided. [708 G H] (3) The word "final" in article 133 (1)(b) means an interlocutory order passed in a proceeding and not final. In the present case, the expression " final order" is an interlocutory one and is final decision of the High Courts. An Order passed by a High Court in appeal against an order of the subordinate court may become infructuous as it has to be determined by the courts in the ordinary way. [070 B C] (4) The question whether a complaint should be filed or not must be decided on its own merits and not on merits. [700 E F] Ramchand Manjimal vs Goverdhandas Vishindas Ratan Chand, ; , followed.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975 he was confirmed with effect from April 1, 1975. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act 1973 came into force on June 13, 1973. Section 33 of the Amending Act provided that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1 1973 and who were in service at the commencement of the amending Act shall continue to be service on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the Panchayats Samiti from time to time. The appellant was confirmed as a head clerk on March 14. 1975. He filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, asking that he should be absorbed as a Sub Clerk. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that by reason of section 14(4) of the Act the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appointment of the petitioner to the post of a Head clerk in the Loharam or the further fact that he was appointed on April 1. 1975 cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13 1973 being the date on which the Panchayat Samities lost its power to making appointments to Panchayat. [738C D] 1.2 The appointment to the posts of a head Clerk being without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post or a Head Clerks. He is appointed lawfully to the Post of a clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. For these reasons, the appeal fails and is dismissed. [38D E] 2.1 It could not, therefore, have been appointed by the appellant as a sub Clerk on April, 1, 1974. The appointment was without authority of Law. [ 737E F] 2:2 Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant was entitled to be consid ered for promotion but whether the Panchayat Sabha had the right in the matter for simple reasonthat these appointments are made after July 13, 1974 being the dates on which Panchayat Samiti lost its powers to make appointment to Panchayat [737F G] 2 :3 The appointment is without authority or law.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity and that the income from the properties belonging to the temple and the deity was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiva Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saana and Saradakar. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the Amauli properties had been purchased by the Math, that Sadasiv Yati being in possession of the property as Mahant, and that he was entitled to possess, enjoy and acquire personal property. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The fund from which the Amaulty properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivshankar Yati. On his death in 1917, all those properties and wealth devolved on him. He was granted a succession certificate by the District Judge, Varanasi, in respect of two fixed deposits made by him in the Bank of Bengal. Mahant Shiv Sakaran Yati executed a will in 1956 bequeathing various properties to the deity with the intent that arrangements for bhog, deepdan and other expenses be met from them. The surplus, the deed directed was to be employed for acquiring further property in the name of the deity. The income from these properties was transferred by Mahant Shiv shankar Yatapani to his predecessor in interest and he was granted the succession certificate. The High Court held that the fund fromwhich the Ama was acquired constituted a personal property and must, therefore, be regarded as property belonging to Math or the temple of the Math.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They applied for a settlement of their lands with the respondent who was an evacuee. The allotment was made in 1949 and the allotment was confirmed on October 31, 1952. On January 6, 1951, the Custodian cancelled the allotment of land in favour of the appellants. In September 1952, the appellants filed a revision application against the order cancelling their allotment. The Additional Custodian dismissed the revision application holding that r. 74 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules 1955 stood in the way of cancellation of the allotment in favour. On appeal by the appellants the Additional Custodian held that r, 74 was not applicable to them as they had been given a right to cancel an allotment under the provisions of section 10 of the Act. The appellants then moved the High Court for a writ quashing the order of the Additional custodian cancelling their allotments and also prayed for a direction to the Additional Deputy Custodian to restore the allotment made in favour them. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the jurisdiction of the Custodian under the , was not affected by the provisions Of sections 12(2) and 19 of the 1954 Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Custodian had no power to cancel the allotment for reasons stated in the section. He could not therefore make out a new case at this stage of argument. [338 B] (ii) The provisions of sections 12 and 19 are subject to rules made under the Act and the Rules made thereunder. Therefore, they must prevail over the general provision in section 10(1). B C] (iii) The contention that there was no entrustment in fact of this property or this class of properties to a managing officer or managing corporation could not be accepted. [336 D] (iv) The appellants had lost their possession before the publication of the notification under section 12(1) of the Indian , and were thus not entitled to the protection of section 19(1 ) of the 1955 Act. [333 E] (v) The fact that the acquired properties had ceased to be evacuee properties, el. (d) of r. 102 permits the managing officer to cancel allotment for any other sufficient reason to be recorded in writing. The only effect of r, 102 is to permit cancellation of an allotment for reason stated. That is all.

The State Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Care) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional AII of Girls School in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale ( Mustait 's Branch) and submitted a corrigendum on June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, the advertisement inviting applications from the eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published by the State Government on June 6, 1985, which was published in June 1985. In the meantime, the State Public Services Commission had undertaken the recruitment to the post. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Service Com mission cancelling the entire recruitment examination and asked for re holding of it. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written exami nation, there was no justification for cancellation of the written part of the recruitment examina tions. [126B] 1.2 The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis of the viva voce test and select those who on the date of the selection, had become final and would not be disturbed. [127C D] 2.1 In the instant case, when no defect is pointed out, there could have be appropriately met, by setting down the four years in the process of recruitment and calling for fresh interview. The sole objection being confined to the exclusion of one group of unsuccessful candidates in tho written examination from the interview, there is no justification. [ 127E F] 2:2 When no tice was pointed to set aside the selection and asking the High Court to re hold of it, this court cannot interfere with the action taken by the Public Services Com mission. The selection of two Scheduled Caste candidates and five Backward Class candidates has become final, and would be not disturbed. The State Public service Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years, in the exercise of the power to cancel the entire recruit ment examination and asking a fresh examination of all other eligible candidates, on the ground of the marks obtained by the selected candidates from the interviewed, could have given public cause.

The appellant brought a suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala and that he as mahant of the Gurdwara had two branches one at Landeke in Moga. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. The plea of the appellant that he was a mahant was rejected by the trial court on the ground that he did not know about the death of his father as its lawfully appointed mahant. The High Court held that after taking evidence, the appellant could not be treated as an application for setting aside abatement of the appeal and the ground for setting it aside was that the appellant did not knew about the date of the death. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The suit was filed on the basis that the appel lant as the lawfully appointed Mahant was entitled to manage the properties of the dera at Landa and that the defendant was unlawfully claiming to be the mahant in the Dona and its properties. [488B] 1.2 In the instant case, the suit was for possession and management of the property attached to the Dwara. The appellant could have been continued under Q. 22, r. 10 of the Civil Procedure Code against the person upon whom the interest had devolved. Order 22, rule 10 is based on the principle that trial of a suit cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest of a party in the subject matter of the suit has devolved upon another during the pendency of the Suit but that suit may be continued against the persons acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22 Rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. [489C D] 1:3. The suit against the appellant was not in his personal capacity but in his capacity as de facto mahant, and there was no certainty as to the person who would be elected as mahants to succeed him. The fact that it was after Som Dass died that Shiam Dass was elected to be a mahants of Dera. [490B] 2.1 In the present case, on the death, Shiam Das was sued in his office as a person who claimed to represent the dera as its duly elected Chela. The claim was not therefore in his individual capacity but that he had no right to recover possession of property of theDera.

The Andhra Pradesh State Legislature passed the Andhra Pradesh Motor Vehicles Rules, 1959. The validity of the said Rules was challenged by some persons who had already attained the age of 55 years on the ground that they were violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the amendment to Rule 2 was not justified as it was made in exercise of the power conferred by Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitu tion. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the said amendment was bad because it was arbitrary and unconnected with the object which it sought to achieve. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The amendment made to Rule I in regard to the revision of pay scales was not violative of Article 311(2) of the constitution. [602C] 2. The power to amend the rules carries with it the power to alter them retrospectively. It is well settled that the service rules can be as much amended, as they can be made under the proviso to Article 309 and that, the power cannot be challenged on the grounds that the decision to reduce the age was arbitrary because it is unscientific in the sense that it is not backed by due investigation or by compilation of relevant data on the subject. If reduction of retirement age from 58 to 55 is to be regarded as arbitrary on the basis that it overlooks the advance made in longevity, fixation of retirement at 58 is also not likely to sustain the charge of arbitrariness. [503D E] 3. The object of Rule 2 is to provide for the termination of service of a permanent servant by a mere notice but not an opportunity to the employee to show that he has a right to livelihood. The rule does not contemplate any such thing as a stigma or prejudice against the employee. [401E F] 4. The Government order dated September 17, 19,9,950, specifically stated that the age for compulsory retirement should be raised from 55 to 58 years and that the question of retirement should not be changed once again. The fact that no consideration was given to the plain and direct recruits did not mean that the rule was arbitrary or irrational. [404F G] 5. The decision to increase the age by reducing the age at 58 to 60 years was a valid exercise of legislative power. It was not open to the Government to reduce its power arbitrarily because it had no power to do so. [405H; 405A B] 6.

The appellants are dealers in raw materials in the State of Haryana. They purchased raw materials inside the State and sold them to dealers who, in turn, exported those goods out of India. The Sales Tax Authorities held that the sales effected by the appellants were not sales in the course of export outside India within the meaning of section 5(1) of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (i) to levy tax on raw materials imposed under section 9(1)(b), there can be no levy of purchase tax u/s 9(2); and (ii) to impose tax on the raw materials, which were not specified in Schedule B, there could be no imposition of purchase Tax u/S 9(i). Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The language of section 9 (1)(a) is clear that it does not use the words "within the meaning Of sub section (1) . . . " In other words, the exemption under section 8(1), which has to be given full meaning, in other words the exemption u/r 5(3). [353B] 1.2 The language used in section 9 is wide and includes within the definition of 'turnover ' the purchase value of goods liable to tax under section 6 of the Act but the goods presently in question are not exigible to tax u /s 9, not only as contended for the assessees and held by this Court above but also on the hypothesis as to the invalidity of section 8 (1). [354C D] 1:3. The language is clear contrast between sales falling under sub section(3) and those failing under sub s.(1) and sub section 5 of section 6. [355E F] 2.1 In the instant case, the assessee assessees purchased raw material inside the state of Haryana but paid no tax thereon as they were registered dealers and furnished the declaration forms prescribed under section 24. The department has denied the relief on the short ground that to levy the tax imposed by section 9 of the Punjab General Sales tax Act, it is not necessary for the State to impose purchase tax under s.9(1).

The appellant firm registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, was carrying on business as dealers in cotton of the total value of Rs. 68,493 2 6 and sales of castor oil of the value of RS. 6,47,509 1 6. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim for exemption from tax on the ground that the goods remained their property till they were brought on board the ship and so the sales were exempted under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. On appeal by the appellant, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sellers were not entitled to the benefit of article 286 (1)(a). The High Court in reference held against the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "the time of the export " meant the time when the goods cross the customs barrier and that therefore the exemption under article286(1) will come into operation. Held, that the expression " the time of export " in section 10(b) means the time within which the goods go out of the territorial waters of India. The words " the place of the import" mean the place where the goods are imported and not where they are not a registered dealer. In the present case the goods were on fumes contracts, that is, the goods went to the destination of the goods and the sellers paid the price. The goods were therefore exempted from tax under article 285(1). The words 'the time when they cross the Customs frontier are clearly intended to be used to indicate an intention of the parties that the property in the goods would not pass till after the ship had passed beyond the territorial limits of India, or at the earliest when the ship leaves the port. The word " the goods" in section 8(b), therefore, means the goods which were delivered outside the State of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by the dealer.

The respondent divorced the appellant, a second wife, and a few years later. The first wife filed a suit for maintenance against the appellant under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 alleging that she had transferred the suit premises to the appellant and also the shares of the Co operative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. The trial court held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ per month, but the High Court affirmed this order. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The object of section 125 is to avoid the divorcee from moral and material abandonment manifest in article 39 of the Constitution. [78 C] (2) The appellant 's right to ignore the terms of the said provision does not arise. The compulsive conclusion from a divorce by a husband and his provision of a separate residence as evidenced by the consent decree fills the bill. Do divorcees have to 1) prove mutual consent to live separately; Divorce painfully implies that the husband orders her out of the conjugal home. If law has nexus with life this argument is still born. The appellant can ignore. So the basic condition of neglect to maintain is satisfied. [79 C D] (3) In the normal course an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the Magistrate at the trial level. However, the High court has not spoken at all. Moreover, the husband has not examined himself to prove that he has been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case is that she has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent order. Obviously, he has no case of non neglect. His plea is his right to ignoring. [80 F G] (4) The High Court has not spoke at all to the effect that the parties had agreed to maintain separately. If it was to be over come, the printed text of the particular Code would have been inapplicable and the husband liberated. This is the teleological decoding of the text of section 127. [81 F G; 80 A] (5) The wife has not explained the circumstances in which she situation was situation. She has not stated that her husband had been giving allowance to the divorce wife. Her case, on the contrary, is that her claim has been forfeited because of the divorce and consent decree.

The Collector of the district after considering the representation made by the appellant, cancelled the order of the Collector. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order. The High Court dismissed the petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the Collector and that there was no requirement for giving any prior notice before black listing any person. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The black listing of the appel lant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law. [868C] 1.2 In so far as the cancellation of the bid of the petitioner is concerned, that is not affected. This order will however not prevent the State Government or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for supervening public business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. [886D E] 1:3 The High court was not justified in interfering with the impugned order. It is an implied principle of the rule of law that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justi ficum. It has to be realised that black listing no person in respect o f business ventures has civil consequences for the future business of a person concerned, in any case. Even assuming that the rules did not express any so, the High Courts will have jurisdiction to pass any order in accordance with law indicating the reasons therefor.

The appellant was the tenant of certain premises in Madras. The first lease deed provided that the lessee shall not be evicted whether in execution of a decree or otherwise except in accordance with the provisions of the lease deed. The second lease provided for a monthly rent of Rs.200 p.m. The appellant filed an eviction petition under section 4(1) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 on the ground that he was the landlord of the entire property covered by the lease. The Rent Controller held that the building on the land leased to the appellant would be conveyed to the L.I.C. for a period of two years and thereafter the rent payable under the lease was Rs.150 p. m. On appeal, the appellate court confirmed the order of eviction. In second appeal, it was contended before this Court that since the subject matter of the tenancy under the deed was only a vacant site, the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation of fair rent in respect of the property which was only an vacant site and therefore the claim by India Automobiles was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question whether the denial of the landlord 's title by the tenant is bona fide or not depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. If the Rent Control Act applies to a particular area, it will have to be established that the person seeking eviction or fixation of rent is in,,, a "landlord" who has, prima facie, the right to receive the rents of the premises in question. [561E F] 1.2 The jurisdiction of the Rent Court is not barred by section 12(4) of Act. But his jurisdiction is a statutory jurisdiction which is vested in the Rent control ler by the terms of the Act. It is not open to the High Court to entertain a collateral attack on the validity of binding nature or correctness of the order passed by the Court of Small Causes and to consider and determine afresh the issue as to whether the Lee has title to the property. [560F G] 1:3. The jurisdiction under section 11(4), as it stood at the relevant time, is a "jurisdiction" which is conferred on the Rent controller by the term of the statute. It will be anomalous to hold that where an owner files a suit for arrears of rent, it is open to him to seek eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil court but that the owner cannot have a similar right in the matter of recovery of rent which is basically a relief for which he has to approach a civil Court. [559G H] 1 :4. The question on which the jurisdiction of civil court is excluded is only the determination as to the fair rent of the land. If, and only if this relationship exists between the parties, the rent Controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the fair price is and then fades out of the picture. Where a fair rent is fixed by a Controller, the landlord has to deal with this incidentally but this is not one of the direct issues before the Rent Magistrate.

The Mysore State Civil Service Integra tion Rules, 1960 provide for filing objections only against the preliminary provisional inter State Seniority List and do not provide any provision for filing objection or appealing against final Inter State Seniority list as per Annexure 'B '. The petitioner was given ample opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. He challenged the validity of the Rules on the ground that they were violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962 so far as category 6 is concerned was ultra vires and illegal and quashed the same. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) a person whose seniority is to be determined under Section 115 of the , must be given an opportunity to make representation against the proposed assigned ment; (ii) the rules had not been complied with in as much as they were not complied with, and (iii) the Rules had not become invalid on account of non compliance with Article 16. HELD: The combined final list dated 4th April 1962 so insofar as category No 6 is con cerned was ultra rites and illegal. [830 D] Shankariah 's case ; , followed. In the instant case, the petitioner respondent was unrepresented, and he had been unable to make out in his petition any grounds for interference with the final list. [828 E F] Shankariah ' case ; referred to. (i)(a) The petitioner respondent had ample opportunity of making a representation against tho final list and the Central Government had also to give him those representations a proper consideration to those representations. So long as the Central Govern ment has acted properly according to the provisions of the Act, it is not inviolable. [829 G] (b) The High Courts have held that a person who is given a reasonable opportunity to be heard against the proposal for proposed assign ing a place cannot be heard, against the impugned list. The principle recognised in Shankariha 's Case was confined to the facts of that case and did not mean that if a final list is prepared contrary to the rules applicable or is vitiated on some ground showing that a condition precedent to the finalisation of the list is absent, it would still be invio ly open to challenge by Courts. [827 G H] (c) The contention that the petitioner had ample opportunities to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by him was not correct. [826 A B] Shanabhaga Prasad vs Ram Chand & Ant. ; , referred to and distinguished.

The petitioners are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the year 1978 79 provided that the Export Houses and Trading Houses would be eligible to Additional Licences on the basis of one third of the f.o.b. value of the exports made in 1977 78, but they could not avail theeconomibilities in import of items granted under clauses (ii) and (iii) of sub para (4) of Para 218 of the Import & Exports Policy 1988 91. The petitioners submitted application for renewal of their Export Houses ' licence on the ground that the export Houses who were issued Additional licences prior to April 1, 1988 could directly import items which were excluded from the Export House 's Licence 1978 79 and the Export Control Policy 198891. On the basis that they had failed to achieve the export exports, the petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay challenging the validity of sub Para 218 read with para 218 of Import & Ex Export Policy 1988 1991. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the grantees of Additional Licences were not only prohibited from importing items which are excluded under the Export Policy 1978 79 but also from importing articles which were specifically banned under the prevalent import policy at the time of import, and that the petitioners who were granted Additional licences in 1977 could not be said to be persons similarly circumstanced as Export Houses who exported goods in the year 1987 88 and in subsequent years and obtain Additional Licences for a much larger amount at a high percentage on the exports effected during the period 1977 78. The writ petition filed by the petitioners was dismissed by the High court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The licences issued to the Trading Houses under the Import and Export Policy of 1978 79 are valid for a period of twelve months and the said period has expired during the pendency of these writ petitions. Since the basis for the grant of Additional licences which are entitled to this relaxation is different from the basis on which Additional Licences had been granted to the petitioners, the Petitioners cannot claim the benefit of the same relaxation and assail the validity or sub para 218 in respect of sub paras (10) of para 218. [248B C] 1.2 The licences granted to Trading Houses, like the petitioners would be permissible if the import policy prevailing at the date of import permits them to import such items. [249C D] 1:3. In view of the fact that the licence issued in favour of M/s. A.J.S.V. Mills Ltd., had been renewed for an Additional Licence whereunder, it is permissible to import items as per para 215 of the Imports & Exports policy 1988 91, the said facility has been denied to the Petitioners and that they have been subjected to arbitrary and hostile discrimination. [250D E] 1 :4.

The appellant is a manufacturer of excisable goods and after completion of its manufacture, it is stored in the storage tank for goods manufactured by it. The appellant has filed price lists in respect of the same. In the price list, which were duly approved by the Asstt. Collector, the appellant had shown the value of fusel oil/styrene monomer irrespective of whether these were supplied by the buyer or not. The Assistant Collector rejected the price lists on the ground that the process of packing was complete and it is the fully manufactured product that is to be sold in packed condition and the containers were not returnable to by the buyers, there fore, the value had to be included in the assessable value. The appeal filed before the Customs, Excise & Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal failed. Hence this appeals by the appellant. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The cost of packing envisaged in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act for determining the "value" in relation to any excisable goods is only the "cost of such pack ing" incurred by the manufacturer and recovered by him from the purchaser except where the packing is of a durable nature and is returnable by the seller to the manufacturer. [995B C] 1.2 The cost incurred by a manufacturer and collected by him on his own cost, is liable to be excluded in the value for the purpose of excise duty. However, if any special secondary packing is provided by the assessee at the in stance of a wholesale buyer which is not generally provided as a normal feature of the wholesale trade, the cost of such special packing would not be includible in the valuation of goods. [996C D] 1:3 The cost for packing envisaged under section 4 (4)(a) is such cost incurred on the assessee and recovered from the buyer except where packing is "of a duable nature and returnable to the manufacturers". The proper interpretation to be placed on the words of section 4 is that every kind of container in which it can be said that the excisable goods are contained would be 'packing ' within the meaning of the Explanation. [994D E] 1 :4. In construing section 4, the Court has to consider the wider proposition canvassed by the two sides and decide whether the cost ously packing referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that while generally the normal price for which the goods are sold at the factory gate is to he taken as the assessablevalue, an addition thereto has to be made where, in addition to the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Headclerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued, he arranged a trap. As instructed by PW 1, the appellant was ready with ten rupees currency notes. The appellant was charged under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the appellant under section 5.(2) of that Act and sentenced him to undergo R.I. for 15 months under section five(2). On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to a period of one year. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the appel lant had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient, the explanation offered by the appellant being probable and there is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appellant had been guilty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction under section 165 I. P.C., and section S(2), read with Section 5(1)(e) of Prevention of Corpo ration Act are unsustainable. [337B] 2. The evidence of PWs 1 to 3 is sufficient to hold the appellant guilty. The prosecution has even failed to prove that the money was the money returned by PW l, the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the prosecution and the presumption, if any, arising under section 4 is rebutted and the conviction cannot therefore be sustained. [340C D] 3. The explanation offered for the appellant 's refusal was probable and that there had been no conclusive evidence to hold him guilty. [341F] 4. The High Court thought that though the conviction under Section 161 I P. C. and sen tence of 5( 2) read along with section S1)(a) of P.W. 337, was to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I.p.C.[334G] Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1964 SC 575; C.I./ Ernden vs State, AIR 1954 Saurashtra 12 1; and Lohana Kantilal vs State AIR 1954 Guj. 12; referred to.

The respondent company was in dire need of the flat in question for its use as a factory. The Company had been in dire necessity of the premises and employees of a company. A letter was addressed to the company on May 21, 1974 to permit him to continue to live in the company 's premises during the period of his employment. On September 26, 1984 the company issued a letter requesting the company to permit the petitioner to continue in its premises during its accumulated period of six months after his retirement and in accordance with the company "s rules". The Company refused to grant permission on the ground that there was acute shortage of housing accommodation in the Metropolitan City of Bombay. The company filed a complaint against the petitioner under section 630 of the Companies Act, 1971 before the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, 37th Court, Esplanade, Bombay alleging that he was wrongfully withholding the flat and had instituted false and frivolous proceedings with ulterior motive to obtain an injunction from the court. The Magistrate took cognizance of the complaint against him under section 6(1) of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act 1971. The petitioner filed a revision petition before the High Court which allowed the same holding that it was not open to the Company to buy property in Bombay for this purpose. The High Court also held that the words "any such property" in section 630(l)(b) relate to any property of a Company as mentioned in cl.(a) i.e. property wrongfully obtained by an officer or employee of the company and therefore, the provisions contained in section 630(1)(b), must be read together. The present petition under article 226 of the Constitution has been filed on behalf of the petitioner challenging the order of the Magistrate. On behalf of respondent it was contended that the provision contained in s.630(l) is a penal provision and therefore must be subject to a strict construction and there is no room for intendment. It was further submitted that the legislature never intended to include past officers and employees in cl. (b) of sub section (1) for the contention that cl. 3(1), (a) and (b), are separated by the word 'or ' and therefore are clearly disjunctive.

The appellant, a public religious trust, was appointed as the trustee of the temple in the year 1817. The trust was to be a public trust and not a private property. The appellant claimed that the Sansthan was a private trust and was entitled to the properties and the said temple was held by the Maharaj who happened to be holding the Gadi at the relevant time. The Assistant Charity Commissioner, after issuing notice to the appellant, held that the appellant was a public charitable trust and directed its registration as a public institution under the Act. The High Court in appeal set aside the order of the District Judge and held that it was a Public Trust and not private property and that the application for a certificate under section 66 of the Act was made ex abundanti cautela. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was not right in giving due importance to the admission of the constituted attorney of the appellant as well as the evidence produced on behalf of the respondent. [523 B] (2) The definition of public trust is a very wide term and includes all persons who are entitled to worship at the shrine, or by any section thereof as a place of public religious worship. The expression "public trust" in section 2(13) means a place by whatever designation known and used as a whole designation or part of it.

The appellant was the sole proprietor of a business carried on under the name and style of Indestro Sales and Service Co. Ltd., Bombay, carrying on business and had its registered office in Bombay. The Income tax Officer issued a recovery certificate to the Additional Collector of Bombay for the recovery of the assessed amount of tax. The appeal against that order was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but the same was allowed by the Collector under section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the recovery certificate on the ground that section 46 (2) Of the Indian Incometax Act, read with section 46 of the Act had no application to the Union and that section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that section 16 of the said Act did not violate article 21 of the Constitu tion as it offended article 14 Of the Constitution inasmuch as the appellant had been arrested and detained in execution of a warrant of arrest issued under section 13 Of the Bombay Act by the Additional Collec tor of Bombay and the Collector had reason to believe that the defaulter was wilfully withholding payment or had been guilty of fraudulent conduct in order to evade payment. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The assessment proceedings had been started and the certificate had been issued by the Income tax officer to the Addl. Collector of the High 'Court under section 45(2), which was a later amendment of the section. [903 B] (ii) Section 46(1) of Bombay City Revenue Act is not violative of Article 14 of tile Constitution inasmuch it does not impose any restriction on the power conferred by article 14. The provisions of the State laws which prescribe that machinery are not incorporated in section 46, do not indicate a different and alternative mode of recovery from the object sought to be achieved by the Act. [804 G] (iii) The procedure prescribed by section 13 is one and the same and it is levied under a single Central Act and yet the ultimate coercive processes for recovery differ in nature and extent between State and State. [085 B C] (iv) The provisions in the Bombay Municipal Land Revenue Code, 1876, as if those provisions were set out in the Indian income tax Act in extenso and form part of the same transaction are not ultra vires article 14 or article 21. [095 E F] (v) The contention that section 17(2)(a) of Act by itself does not violate Article 14 is without substance because the impugned law was based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus with the object of the particular public laws which prescribes a procedure for recovery of arrears of land revenue. [105 B D] (vi) The classification has been made on intelligible differentia and the subjection, for the purposes of the various sections of the Income Tax Act, is not arbitrary or discriminatory. [1004 C] Bhikaji Narayan Dhakras vs The Collector of Malabar, ; , followed. (vii) The levy of tax being a subject with respect to which the Union alone may make law and yet another State cannot complain of denial of equal protection of laws on the grounds of discrimination.

The respondent company was a registered firm and the members of the said company were represented by its Trustees. The respondents contended that under a scheme of 12hour shift with 8 hours ' work, overtime should be at least 3 hours if not 4 hours in the ordinary working day. The Tribunal held that the company was not able to establish that the existing system of work required any modification and that the period of rest was illusory since being variable it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some times at the end depending on the tact. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The hours of work in a six day week should be so arranged that inclusive of intervals for rest would not spread over more than 12 hours. The normal working day thus includes periods of inaction during which the employee may be on duty but is not called upon to display either physical activity or sustained attention. The provisions of section 13(2) (c) read with section 13 (3) give an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest. If it is the latter, it is counted as actual work period. [638 F G] (ii) On any single day the number of hours of working must not exceed 9 and together with the hours of rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours in a day. A working day may extend to 12 hours but the number is reduced by the time given for the purpose. The expression " inclusive of one or more specified intervals" governs the normal working days and not the number or hours of leave.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in which accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika. The respondent landlord filed a suit against the appellant for eviction on the ground that the shop and the basement were separately let out to the appellant and the same were not separately let into the premises. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to protection under section 20 of the Act because the shop was let out in June 1976 but as the assessment was made on October 1, 1976 the provisions of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 would not apply for ten years from October 1.76. The appellant filed an appeal before the Additional District Judge who allowed the same holding that since the premises were let out on June 25, 1976, the provisions under the Act will not apply to them. The High Court also held that the right of parties will be governed by the U P. Urban Building (Regulation) Act 1972 and therefore a decree for eviction could only be passed after the expiry of ten years i.e. 1st October, 1976. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since in view of the language of section 39 and 40 of the new Rent Act, provisions of this Act will apply to the present case and therefore the benefit of the old Act would not be available to the tenant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The rights of parties are determined on the basis of the rights available to them on the date of the suit, but in Vineet Kumar vs Mangal Sain Wadhera Dass Dassi & Ors., ; this Court took the view that if during the pendency of the proceedings in this Court even of 10 years expired the protection will not be attracted as the suit has been instituted within ten years and therefore restriction as provided for in section 20 can not be invoked. [164F G] 1.2 The rights cannot be defeated by a decree of the court, efflux of time or on the expiration of a notice to quit or in any other manner. It is true that the appeal is the continuation of the litigation even of the 10 years. However, this Court would not ordinarily interfere with the order of eviction unless it is shown that the provisions contemplated in those sections are satisfied.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of the appellant from the property in dispute on the ground that he was thika tenants under him. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had not made any grounds for eviction and that the Act as amended by the West Bengal Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, did not apply to pre Act suits and the suit was not governed by the Thika Tenants ' Protection Act, 1949. On appeal the High Court held that the trial court had no jurisdiction to pass a decree as the respondent was a thika tenant within the meaning of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) since the suit had been filed before the Act but was not disposed of by that date, the landlord had to establish that he is entitled to possession because of the existence of any of the grounds mentioned in section 3; and (ii) even if no proceedings were pending in any court, it was open to the thika tenancy to eject a thikka tenant on the basis that the applicant was a Thika tenant. HELD: (i). The provisions of the Calcutta Thika Tenant ' Protection Ordinance 1952, as amended upto 1953, apply to all suits and proceedings which were pending at the date of commencement of the 1949 Act. [179 E] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed. (ii).The respondent was entitled to the benefit of section 4 of the West Tenancy Act, 1948 as amended up to 1953, because the landlord made no attempt to establish any of these grounds for ejectment mentioned in s.3. The decision of the High COurt is right inasmuch as the landlord has not established any of those grounds specified in section 4.

The State Government appointed a Pay Commission to consider the duties and responsibilities of different categories of posts. The Committee recommended that the number of total posts in the concerned cadre should be increased from 10, 300 to 30 per cent of the total cadre strength. The recommendation was accepted by the Government and the order dated July 2, 1976 was issued by the State Government appointing the Pay Commission as a result of sanction of this scale. The High Court took the view that the post of Bench Secretaries Grade I was not equivalent to a post in the higher pay scale and that it offends Article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the creation of two grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Secretary who were doing the same or similar work is violative of Articles 14; (ii) the constitution of the Pay Commis sion Committee did not disturb the categorisation of Bench Assistants into Grade I and Grade II. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" has to be construed in the first place. It cannot be denied that the quality of work performed by persons of longer experience is superior than the work of newcomers. [302E] 2. The differentiation so made in the same cadre will not amount to discrimination. The classification based on experience is a reasonable classification. To hold otherwise, it would be detrimental to the interest of the service itself. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment emphasise that equal pay for unequal work will be a negation of that right. And said: "The principle of 'equal pay ' for equal works has to he construed in tho first place". [303G H] 3. The distinction so made is not violative of the right to have equal pay. [304H] Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. 4. The State Government has granted uniform pay scale of Rs. violate Article 14. After the argument was concluded in this appeal, counsel on both sides brought to our attention that the State Govern ment has granted similar pay scale to both the grades of Bench Execu tive Officers with effect from January 1, 1986. When Bench Secretaries grade may do the same work, but their quality of duty may differ. Under the rules framed by the Chief Justice of the High Court, Bench Secretaries are selected by a Selection Committee. The selection is based on merit with due regard to seniority. They are selected among the lot of Bench represen tatives Grade II and when the matter was concluded, counsel for both sides bring to our notice that counsel on either side brought to the notice that the High Courts completely overlooked the criterion provided under the Rules. [303H; 304A B] 5. The merit governs the grant of higher pay scales and that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority.

The appellant companies challenged the validity of the demand for property tax made by it on the ground that no tax was leviable on its property since the Company was owned wholly by the Government of India and that respondent No 1 had no right to levy the property tax. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 or section 135 of the Municipal Act did not contain any independent provision or machinery for exercising the power of taxation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant companies that (i) since the appellant Companies were wholly owned by the State Government and were taken on lease for a period of 30 years by the appellant company, the lands and buildings owned by it could not be subjected to property tax; (ii) since sugar was a declared industry under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951, Parliament alone was competent to pass the impugned Act by virtue of Entry 23 of List II. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The State Legislature enacted the Act of 1973. It was further held that the land cess was not a tax on mineral rights but was in truth and substance a "tax on lands" within the meaning of Entry 49 of the State List. [19A B] 2.1 In order to 20 judge whether, on that account, the State Legislature loses its competence to pass Act of1973 it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that Act and to the relevant provisions thereof under which Special Area Development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and building within their jurisdiction. [20D E] 2:2 The legislative field covered by Entry 23, List II will pass on to Parliament by virtue Of Entry 54, List I. But in order to exercise the powers conferred by that entry, the legislature must be construed as limited in its scope so as not to come in conflict with the power and function of the Union to regulate and develop the mines as envisaged by the Nationalisation Act. [21E F] 2I2 In order that a law may be passed on the subject, it must be interpreted as limited by the language used and not to be read in isolation. The true meaning behind the words "any State" is not to do with the development of mines. The power conferred by the Constitution on Special Area Authority to impose the property taxes on lands and premises is therefore not in conflictwith the power conferred under the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act on the Union Government to regulate or develop the coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. [22F G] 2l3 The State legislature has the competence to enact the impugned law. It cannot, however, pass a law which is inconsistent with the powers and function conferred by Parliament. [23G H] 3.1 The power of the legislature under Entry 24, List 11 will be exercised not only in respect to land but also for the purpose of development.

The appellant was granted a lease of certain slate quarries in his estate for five years in respect of which he had made an application to the Collector under r. 476 of the Rules framed under the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, for setting aside the grant on the ground that the lease was for a period exceeding one year. The appellant contended that the leases were granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, for a certain period and that the lessee had not given three months ' notice to the Government before the expiry of the lease. Held, that the words " such rights" in the third proviso to section 20(1) of the Act refer to rights created after July 1. 1945, but these words occur in the second proviso only when they are used for a limited period and not with reference to the period prior to the expiry. The effect of the second Proviso is that the Government must do something to avoid them. The third proviso does not govern the second or the third provisos. A lease granted by a private person for a specified period cannot be terminated merely on the fulfilment of certain conditions mentioned in the first proviso and it cannot be said that the appellant had formed the opinion that it was in the public interest to terminate the transaction. A lessee has created no right in any land under the grant, and he can claim compensation only when his right is terminated by the Government under the second provisos. The second proviso does nothing more than add some terms to the lease and the words 'such rights refer in the body of the section, and those words occurren in the fourth proviso. A. M.
